# THE GATE OF LANGUAGES UNLOCKED: <note>original Latin: "Janua Linguarum Reserata"</note>

## OR A SEED-PLOT <note>original: "Seminarium"</note> of all Sciences and Languages:

-> THAT IS, <-

-> A brief method for learning Latin and English, and other languages, as well as the foundations of the arts; together with the <term>Vestibule<note>Latin: "Vestibulo." In Comenius's educational system, the Vestibule was an introductory primer intended to precede the more difficult Janua.</note></term> of the Gate of Latinity. <-

-> *By the famous* J. A. COMENIUS. <-

<summary>This is the title page for the 1641 English edition of John Amos Comenius's revolutionary language-learning manual, which combined linguistics with the study of sciences and arts. It credits the original author alongside translators Thomas Horn and John Robotham, highlighting its role as a comprehensive pedagogical tool.</summary>

# *The Gate of Latinity* <note>original: "Janua Latinitatis"</note>
## *The Portal.* <note>original: "Vestibulum"</note>

**C**ome, children.
Learn the Latin language,
Beautiful & elegant.
Grasp it
According to your capacity,
And various things—
The seeds of wisdom.
God will help you.
Teachers will love you.
Others will praise you.
You yourselves will rejoice.
If the beginning is difficult,
The middle will be easy,
The end pleasant.

---

### CHAPTER I.
#### On the properties of things. <note>original: "De accidentibus rerum." In historical philosophy, "accidents" refer to the characteristics or attributes of a thing that are not part of its essential nature, such as size or location.</note>

**G**od is eternal.
The world is temporary.
An angel is immortal.
<unclear>H</unclear>umanity is mortal.
<unclear>C</unclear>orpus is visible.
<unclear>S</unclear>pirit is invisible.
<unclear>T</unclear>he soul is likewise.
<unclear>H</unclear>eaven is the highest.
<unclear>T</unclear>he air is in the middle.
<unclear>T</unclear>he earth is the lowest.
<unclear>A</unclear> cloud is remote.
<unclear>A</unclear> mist is near.
<unclear>A</unclear> place is large or small.
<unclear>T</unclear>ime is long or short.
<unclear>A</unclear> space <note>original: "Area"</note> is wide or narrow.
<unclear>A</unclear> house is spacious or cramped.
<unclear>M</unclear>ountains are high.

<meta>This page continues Chapter 2 of John Amos Comenius's language primer, "The Portal to the Gate of Tongues." # The Portall to the Gate of Tongues.

### Of the Elements. <note>original: "Elementorum." In the 17th century, the "elements" referred to earth, air, fire, and water, which were believed to be the building blocks of all matter.</note>
The elements nourish us.
Fire burns.
The flame blazes.
A spark glows.
Thunder thunders.
The wind blows.
Rain rains.
Snow snows.
Water flows on a level surface.

It flows from a vessel.
It leaps from a fountain.

It is drawn from a well.

### Of Plants. <note>original: "Plantarum."</note>
An herb grows.
A leaf is green.
A flower blooms.
The fruit ripens.
So that you may pluck it,
Bend the branch.
Whether they be pears, or plums, or cherries, etc.
A nut contains a kernel.
A rose smells sweet.
A nettle burns.

### Of Animals. <note>original: "Animalium."</note>
A stone lies still.
A tree stands.
A living creature moves itself.
A bird flies.
A fish swims.
A four-footed beast walks.
A serpent slithers.
A worm crawls.
A deer runs.
A horse neighs.
An ox lows.
A lamb bleats.
A pig (or sow) grunts.
A bear growls.
A wolf howls.

<column-break/>

### Of the Elements.
*The elements do nourish us.*
*The fire burns.*
*The flame flashes.*
*A spark glows.*
*Thunder thunders.*
*The wind blows.*
*The rain rains.*
*The snow snows.*
*The water runs on the level*
*(ground).*

*It flows out of a vessel.*
*It bubbles (or leaps) out of a*
*fountain.*

*It is drawn out of a pit.* <note>The "pit" here refers to a well-shaft.</note>

### Of Plants.
*An herb increases.*
*A leaf is green.*
*A flower flourishes.*
*The fruit waxes ripe.* <note>"Waxeth" means "becomes" or "grows."</note>
*Which that thou mayest crop,*
*Bend the bough.*
*Whether they be pears, or plums,*
*or cherries, etc.*
*A nut contains a kernel.*
*A rose smells well.*
*A nettle stings (burns).*

### Of living creatures.
*A stone lies along.*
*A tree stands up.*
*A living creature moves itself.*
*A bird flies.*
*A fish swims.*
*A four-footed beast goes.*
*A serpent creeps.*
*A worm crawls.*
*A hart runs.* <note>A "hart" is an archaic term for a male red deer.</note>
*A horse neighs.*
*An ox lows.*
*A lamb bleats.*
*A hog (sow) grunts.*
*A bear murmurs.*
*A wolf howls.*

# The Portall to the Gate of Tongues.

*A dog barks.*
*A ram butts.*
*A wild beast tears in pieces.*
*A hare flees.*
*A fox changes his coat.* <note>The original English uses "haires" to refer to the fox's fur.</note>
*A cat catches mice.*
*A hen lays eggs.*
*A goose eats oats.*
*Worms gnaw fatty things.*
*Lice bite the skin.*
*As also gnats and fleas.*
*An ant is industrious.*
*A spider is skillful.* <note>The original word "artificiall" here means "full of art" or "crafty," referring to the spider's ability to weave webs.</note>
*Bees prick with their sting.*
*Whatever lives is vigorous.*

### Of Man.

*We do various things.*
*With body and mind.*
*The head is filled with the brain.*
*It is covered with hair.*
*(Except for the face.)*
*No limb is given in vain.*
*For we see with the eyes.*
*We clear out waste through the nose.*
*The forehead has wrinkles.*
*The ears hear.*
*The nostrils smell.*
*The tongue tastes how things*
*savour.* <note>The text uses "favour," an archaic spelling for "savour," meaning to have a specific taste.</note>
*We chew with the teeth.*
*The stomach digests.* <note>The original word "concocteth" refers to the old medical belief that digestion was a process of "cooking" food with internal heat.</note>
*The bowels cast out waste.*
*The liver makes blood, and sends*
*it through the veins.* <note>At the time of writing, the liver was believed to be the primary organ for creating blood.</note>
*The heart beats.*
*The lungs breathe.*
*The lips are around the mouth.*
*A beard adorns the chin.*
*Women are beardless.*
*We carry on the shoulders.*
*We embrace with the arms.*
*We labor with the hands.*
*The left holds, the right performs*
*the work.*

A dog barks. <note>original: "Canis latrat."</note>

### Of Man. <note>original: "Hominis."</note>

We do various things. <note>original: "Nos agimus varia."</note>
By body and mind.
The head is filled with the brain.
It is covered with hairs.
(Except for the countenance.)
No limb is given in vain.
For we discern with the eyes.
We excrete through the nose.
The forehead has wrinkles.
The ears hear.
The nostrils smell.
The tongue tastes how things
taste. <note>original: "sapiant."</note>
We chew with the teeth.
The stomach digests.
The intestines discharge.
The liver creates blood, and
distributes it through the veins.
The heart throbs.
The lung breathes.
The lips are around the mouth.
A beard adorns the chin.
Women are beardless.
We carry things on the shoulders.
We embrace with the arms.
We work with the hands.
The left hand holds, the right finishes
the work.

<meta>This page continues the elementary survey of the human condition begun on the previous page. # The Portall to the Gate of Tongues.

We stroke with the palm. <note>original: "Palma palpamus"</note>
We strike with the fist.
We grasp with the hollow of the hand.
We bind things with the fingers.
We scratch and scrape with the nails.
The belly is beneath the chest.
The sides are below the armpits.
The ribs are beneath these.
The back has shoulder blades above, and loins below.
We sit on the buttocks.
We walk with the feet.

### *Of the Mind.*

The mind always thinks of something.
Even in sleep it dreams.
The understanding understands.
Reasoning reasons.
Memory remembers.
And if it has forgotten anything, it recalls it.
The will wants what is good.
It turns away from evil.
But it is often deceived.
It rejoices and is saddened.
The secure person cares for nothing.
The safe person fears nothing.
The vigorous person works.
The weary person rests.
For wakefulness tires.
Deep sleep restores.
When you have slept seven hours
and wake up, rouse others.

### *Of the Sick.* <note>original: "Morbidorum"</note>

One who is fasting desires food.
One who is full is repulsed by it.
One who is fastidious chooses carefully.
One who is sound is in good health.

### Chapter 4.
### Concerning things in a school.

A student frequents the school.
So that he may be educated in the arts.
The beginning is from letters.
Words are composed of syllables.
Speech is composed of words.
We read silently from a book.
Or we recite it clearly.
We wrap it in parchment. <note>Parchment, made from animal skin, was frequently used for book covers to protect the paper within.</note>
And we place it on a desk. <note>original: "pulpito," a raised writing slope or lectern.</note>
Ink is in the ink-horn, in which we dip the quill.
We write with it on paper, on both pages.
If we write wrongly, we delete it.
And we mark it again correctly, or in the margin.
A teacher teaches.
A disciple learns, not all at once, but in stages.
The instructor commands what is to be done.
The Rector rules the Academy.

## TO
# LEARNED READERS
### PREFACE.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter C, decorated with floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>

Reality itself speaks to the fact that the true and natural method of teaching languages has not been sufficiently understood by the Schools until now. Most who had dedicated themselves to letters grew old over mere words. To the Latin language alone, ten or more years were assigned; indeed, a whole lifetime for the slowest learners, and that with thin progress that hardly paid back the effort. Great men long ago complained of this: Vives <note>Juan Luis Vives (1493–1540), a Spanish humanist and educational reformer.</note>, Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam, the famous Renaissance scholar.</note>, Sturm <note>Johannes Sturm, influential Protestant educator known for his school system in Strasbourg.</note>, Frischlin <note>Nicodemus Frischlin, a German philologist and poet.</note>, Dornavius <note>Caspar Dornau, a German physician and scholar.</note>, and others; their complaints on this matter are quite clear, yet their remedies did not uproot the evil at its core. Therefore, the more excellent minds of the Scaligers <note>Julius Caesar and Joseph Justus Scaliger, titan scholars of the late Renaissance.</note>, the Lipsiuses <note>Justus Lipsius, a famous Stoic philosopher and philologist.</note>, and others, having abandoned that unhappily worn-out common path, successfully reached the peaks of languages and sciences through certain winding, yet more direct, trails. But truly, they showed their footprints to few who could follow; and it is not in everyone’s power to attempt unfamiliar things by one's own imagination, or (as they say) "to swim without corks" <note>original: "nare sine cortice"—a Latin idiom meaning to proceed without help or support.</note>.

Because of this, the Schools (whatever they may boast about the happiness of the age and the light of letters) have for the most part retained their disorders <term>ataxias: a Greek-derived word meaning disorder or lack of coordination</term> until now. Youth was indeed distracted, or rather strained, for several years by grammatical instructions that were infinitely long, tangled, obscure, and mostly useless; this was the first torture <note>original: "crux"—literally 'cross', often used to mean a hardship or torment.</note>. Then, through those same years, they were stuffed with words for things without the things themselves <note>This reflects a pedagogical shift toward "Realism," where words are taught alongside the objects they represent.</note>; that is to say, neither were the things shown which were to be expressed by those words (so that a more easy, firm, and clear impression might be made through utility), nor were the connections of words and the power of the language itself shown. This was a manifest error on both sides. For since words are signs of things, what will they signify if the things are unknown? Though a boy may know how to recite thousands upon thousands of words, if he does not know how to apply them to things, what use will that equipment have?

Whoever hopes that a speech can arise from separate words alone might as well hope that sand can be gathered into bundles, or a wall raised from stones without mortar. Therefore, the study of the Latin language is far too hindered by vocabularies and dictionaries. But the "good authors"—Terence, Plautus, Cicero, Virgil, Horace, and others—introduced into schools by the consensus of great men, are thought to heal these noticed inconveniences. This is partly because knowledge of various subjects is acquired from them along with knowledge of the language, and partly because the most pure [purity] <note>original: "pu-", completed by the catchword "ritas" (puritas) on the following page.</note> of Roman speech...

<summary>In this preface, the author critiques traditional Latin education for focusing on abstract grammar and rote memorization of words without context. He argues that language should be taught through "things" and meaningful structure rather than just dictionaries.</summary>

# PREFACE.

<note>original: "PRÆFATIO"</note>

<meta>catchword: per- [perfectum]</meta>
<sig>I</sig>
<sig>B</sig>

<unclear>Truth</unclear> can be drawn most securely from those ancient writers, as if from a true spring. But truly, this custom, though it sounds plausible, is extremely inconvenient. First, for not everyone’s fortune allows them to procure as many authors as are required. Then, to drive youth to such vast volumes of these authors—who are for the most part sublime, beyond the grasp of childhood, and treating matters foreign to our daily use—is like pushing a small boat that only wishes to play in a little stream out into a vast ocean, where it must either be tossed by eternal errors, or swallowed by the waves, or certainly be returned to the shore without any benefit. To this, even if someone were to crawl through all those writers with the greatest effort, they would still find themselves not having attained the goal (namely, a sufficient knowledge of the language), because those authors did not treat all subjects; and even if they had treated all the subjects of their own times, they could not have known or treated ours. Thus, it would eventually be necessary to add, read, and re-read many other writers, both ancient and modern (writers on Botany, Metals, Agriculture, Military matters, Architecture, etc., whom Frischlin <note>Nicodemus Frischlin (1547–1590), a German philologist who argued for learning language through practical nomenclature rather than just poetry.</note> lists in the preface of his nomenclature); certainly, there would be no easy end to accumulating these.

Finally, if someone spends so many years for the sake of learning a language, when will they ever come to <term>real things</term> <note>original: "realia". In 17th-century education, this referred to substantive subjects like science and law, as opposed to "verbalia," the mere study of words.</note>? When will they imbue their mind with the knowledge of a sounder Philosophy? When will they enter the thresholds of most holy Theology? Or seek out the secrets of the Physicians? Or unroll the volumes of the Lawyers? When will they arrive at the end of their studies? And what is more: when will they exercise the practice of such long-sought learning for the good of the Church and the State? Certainly, due to the shortness of this life, they will either never do so, or only very late, finding their life has been consumed by these mere preparations. Therefore, it was to be desired by the prayers of all, that some *Epitome* <note>A condensed summary or abridgment.</note> of the whole language be so constructed that all its words and phrases, reduced into one body, might provide a quick, pleasant, and safe transition to the authors of real subjects in a short space of time and with little labor. For Master Isaac Habrecht <note>A physician and mathematician from Strasbourg who published versions of Comenius's work.</note> truly wrote (though some less prudently apply this to Dictionaries): "Just as," he says, "it would be much easier to recognize all animals by sight by visiting Noah’s Ark, which contained pairs selected from every kind, than by traveling the whole world until one happened upon each animal by chance; in exactly the same way, all words will be learned much more easily from an *Epitome* of the language, in which the foundations of all are contained, than by hearing, speaking, or reading until one falls upon so many words by chance."

A certain man from among the Jesuits noticed this a few years ago; he, having embraced the whole Latin language in one bundle, published (under the title of the Irish College of Salamanca in Spain) the *Gate of Tongues* <note>original: "Janua Linguarum". This refers to a famous textbook first developed by William Bathe, an Irish Jesuit in Spain, which sought to teach Latin through 1,200 non-repeating sentences.</note> in Latin and Spanish. In that work, all the more common words of the Latin language are included in twelve centuries <note>Groups of one hundred.</note> of sentences, and arranged in such a way that none of them (except for small particles like *sum* [am], *ex* [from], etc.) recurs once it has been placed, yet each one is heard in its proper construction and within a graceful phrase.

# PREFACE.
<note>original: "PRÆFATIO"</note>

->A 3<-

This invention, as soon as it was seen by the English, was approved, commended, and even enlarged by the English <note>This refers to the *Janua Linguarum* originally developed by Irish Jesuits in Spain, which was quickly adapted into English versions.</note>, and published in print in the year 1615. Two years later, Master Isaac Habrecht of Strasbourg, a German, added the French language and published a four-language edition in that same place. Once it spread into Germany, he also added a German translation, wonderfully commending this method of teaching and learning languages. Indeed, he calls it the most condensed, certain, useful, and never-sufficiently-praised method. He easily found many supporters for this view. For it has been published in various places in Germany, eagerly distributed, introduced into several well-known schools, and in the year 1629, it was set forth in eight languages.

When this work also came into my hands, I read it through once and twice with great eagerness and pleasure, greatly congratulating the youth that more certain aids for the weakness of the memory were being granted by Divine gift. But a little later, comparing it more attentively with its own goal, I began to doubt whether it truly provides what it promises; and upon a third, more accurate reading with careful judgment, I realized it cannot rightfully maintain its title. What I say here is said truly and without envy, as I shall make clear from the fact that it does not perform the function of a **Gate**.

For does the gate of a house not let those arriving from the outside in? Certainly it does. But this *Gate* of the Irish Fathers <note>original: "Patrum Hybernorum"; referring to the Jesuit scholars at the Irish College in Salamanca who first compiled the *Janua*.</note> contributes little or nothing to beginners who must be introduced to Latin from elsewhere. This is proven for a threefold reason. First, a certain portion of words required for daily use is missing here; on the contrary, many unusual words are brought forth that exceed the grasp and use of beginners. For this reason, some rightly judge that this **Jesuitical Gate** is not so much for instructing language beginners, but rather can be used for testing the progress of those who have moved somewhat forward—especially <term>sciolists</term> <note>original: "Sciolorum"; those with a superficial, "know-it-all" smattering of knowledge.</note> in the Latin language. By this reasoning, it should obtain the name not of a **Gate**, but of a **Back Door**. <note>original: "Postici"</note>

The second thing I find lacking is that since individual words are placed there only once, even <term>polysemous</term> <note>words with multiple meanings</note> and <term>homonymous</term> <note>words that sound the same but have different meanings</note> words (of which the Latin language has a great many, as do other languages) appear only once. How then shall a beginner of Latin be sent from this "Gate of Tongues" into the reading of Authors (for that is the goal of the Gate) if he remains ignorant of so many other meanings for a word? And indeed—which is the third and most important thing I find lacking—it should have at least placed each word in its principal, that is, its first, simple, and native meaning; a sharp mind would more easily scent out the remaining vast meanings. But that was not done. Most words are used figuratively, <term>metaphorically</term>, <term>metonymically</term>, or <term>synecdochically</term> <note>Types of figurative language where words are used outside their literal sense.</note>; for the author hunted for elegance in the sentences almost everywhere. I will say nothing of the shapelessness of many sentences, which offer no use for morals or grammar—indeed, they have no sense, so that the words themselves can hardly be joined together, which is a cause for wonder. (For example: 360. *The shackles are struck onto the craftsman's own feet.* 623. *I found that the guarantor was secretly killed in the workhouse.* 733. *The downfall of the lordship has reached the threshold.* 953. *These...*)

<meta>This page continues the author’s critique and refinement of the *Janua Linguarum* (The Gate of Tongues). Having previously discussed the history of the work, the author now addresses his own motivations for creating a new version that better serves the needs of students by linking language directly to the understanding of things.</meta>

# PREFACE.

(...posthumous webs of words, and the like.)

But because those Fathers <note>The Irish Jesuits who authored the original *Janua Linguarum*.</note> were the first to attempt such a compendium of the whole language, we gratefully acknowledge what was invented; what was erred, we kindly forgive. And because it is not equally difficult to add to inventions as it is to discover new things by the occasion of a single invention, why should we not strive for something **Farther Beyond**? <note>original: "Plus ultra"</note> That most learned man, Master Rhenius <note>Johann Rhenius (1574–1639), a prominent German grammarian and educator.</note>, who has deserved much from the schools, urged that if any of our people perhaps had more leisure at hand, they should not refuse the labor of crafting something more accurately. But it is not yet clear that anyone has set their hand to it. Thus it happened that I, though the last and least, have ventured to try, and have set my mind to supply what I found missing there. Certainly not from any confidence in my own talent or erudition (of which I freely acknowledge and deplore that I have scarcely a shadow), nor because I had an abundance of leisure, but moved by the sole desire to promote the advantage of Youth. What I have either performed or wished to perform here must not be passed over in silence, but exposed both for the instruction of beginners and the judgment of the learned.

1.  Firstly, because among the unshakeable laws of teaching <term>didactics|The art or science of teaching</term> I hold this: that *the Intellect and Language should always run parallel, and as much as one grasps of things, so much should one be accustomed to speak* (for how does one who understands what he cannot express differ from a mute statue? To give forth sounds without a mind is the way of parrots). I thought it necessary that the entire universe of things be digested into certain classes, suited to the grasp of childhood, so that what is to be expressed in speech might first be impressed upon *the resident imaginative part* <note>original: "Residenti imaginativæ parti"; the author refers to the mental faculty that stores sensory images of objects.</note>. And so it was done, and there were born to me a hundred common titles of things.

2.  The next care was to select the more common dictionaries <note>original: "lexica"</note> by unrolling them, and to arrange them for expressing things (for which they were either first invented or later applied) so that nothing necessary was omitted, and nothing left to be sought except in its own place. Therefore, about 8,000 words <note>original: "vocabula"</note> were reduced into a thousand sentences, which I first formed as shorter and single-membered, then longer and multi-membered.

But because we have learned by the testimony of Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and philosopher whose Latin style was the gold standard for Renaissance education.</note> that *it matters much that boys, from their very first years, be accustomed to the proper meaning of words*; and proper words are (as Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo.</note> says in Book 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 10) those used to signify the very things for which they were invented. I have labored anxiously so that, for the first understanding of boys, all words appear in their proper and native significance, with a few exceptions: those that have lost their proper use, or those where proper Latin words were missing to express certain small items (for which constant regard was given).

3.  Having set these boundaries, and following the *Gate* <note>The *Janua Linguarum*.</note> of the Irishmen, I have placed each word only once, except for homonyms <note>Words that sound the same but have different meanings.</note>, which, if their different meanings had to be expressed in different places (namely, in different subject matter), had to be repeated. Regarding connecting particles (*and, but, because, all, etc.*), I hope no one will raise a dispute.

<summary>The author explains his motivation for revising the *Janua Linguarum*, emphasizing the pedagogical principle that language learning must parallel the understanding of physical objects. He details his method of organizing 8,000 words into 1,000 sentences categorized by subject matter to improve student retention and accuracy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author’s preface to his linguistic work, specifically outlining the technical improvements he has made to the structure of the *Janua Linguarum* (Gate of Tongues) to aid students in learning Latin through synonyms, grammar, and etymology.</meta>

# PREFACE

->A 4<-

4. *I have mostly placed **synonyms and opposites** next to each other and arranged them so that one reveals the genuine meaning of the other. However, for those synonyms that signify exactly the same thing and are only rendered by a single word in the native language, I have placed the second one in square brackets and different type:* <note>original: "parenthesi quadratâ & diversis literis"</note> *as in section 40:* **The Morning Star [The Light-bringer]** <note>original: "Luciferum [Phosphorum]"</note> *page 135;* **Elecampane [Inula]** <note>original: "Helenium [Inula]"</note> *page 581;* **Soap [Cleanser]** <note>original: "Sapone [Smegmate]"</note> *etc.*

5. *And so that **Grammar** might also have support, I have established the connection of words in such a way that not only the syntactic construction—wherever it departs from the native language—but also some etymological property (Gender, Declension, Conjugation, etc.) might be hinted at. For example, from section 169:* (**They bring us salted herrings**) <note>original: "Haleces salitas nobis afferunt"</note> *a boy will easily remember that "herring"* <note>original: "halecem"</note> *is feminine gender. From section 420:* (**who eats them?**) <note>original: "quis iis vescatur?"</note> *he will observe that "to eat"* <note>original: "Vesci"</note> *is joined not to the Accusative case, but to the Ablative, etc.* 6. *We have adapted the native language to the Latin so that not only all the roots of both languages, with their more important derivatives and compounds, might stand out in their natural sense as far as possible; but also that the metaphors arising from them may afterwards be understood of their own accord, as if a torch had been applied. However, for this first edition, we have seen to it that the native text is printed separately (since it could not be of use to everyone whose judgment we are now going to test).*

7. *We have also added a **small index** of Latin words, as the **Irish Fathers** <note>The Jesuits at the Irish College in Salamanca, who published the first version of this method in 1611.</note> did, intending to do the same hereafter for the native languages. As a work of greater labor and more significant use, we are also laboring upon an* **ETYMOLOGICAL LEXICON**, *which will provide the reasons for all names, both by uncovering the origins of the roots themselves (whether from Latin, or from Greek and Hebrew sources) and by laying out the series of derivatives before the eyes in a new, succinct, and easy method. We will also add a brief and accurate collection of phrases: likewise a very useful treatise on Homonyms, Paronyms, and Synonyms: and finally, a Grammar arranged for shortcut-like ease and rapid practice, according to the true laws of natural <term>didactics|The systematic study of teaching and learning methods</term>: and even a synopsis of that same teaching method for teachers and learners. All of these, comprised in one volume, could represent a small treasury of primary school learning.*

*We shall therefore seem to have a* **GATE OF TONGUES** <note>original: "JANUAM LINGUARUM"</note> *well-fortified with solid posts (the things themselves), easily opened on swinging hinges (the Lexicon), and readily unlocked with a ready key (the Grammar); we shall have it, I say, as long as nothing more perfected is supplied by more excellent talents. That I have no doubt of this is due not so much to those magnificent promises of **Glaum** and the **Glaumians** <note>Likely referring to a contemporary educator whose ambitious promises had not yet materialized into published results.</note> known to the world (about which nothing is yet certain in reality), but rather to that fervent heat and emulation of many in unearthing the foundations of teaching. Indeed, I already see more exquisite things than these: yet because nearly three years were consumed in arranging them (who would easily believe such a tiny little work cost so much?), and because leisure is not available to demolish them completely and rebuild from scratch,*

--- Page 32 ---
<meta>This page concludes Comenius’s preface. He transitions from technical linguistic details to his broader educational philosophy, explaining his hope that this "Nursery" of language will provide a foundation for learning, morality, and piety. He also notes that he is writing from exile in 1631.</meta>

# PREFACE

*...it pleased me to bring these things to light in the form they have now been prepared: if for no other reason than that someone else, endowed with richer talent and learning, might dare something greater, perhaps even having received a spark from these efforts of ours. Therefore, let it be enough to have tested the new waters <note>original: "tentasse vadum," literally "to have tried the ford"</note> and to have broken the new ice.*

*It seemed better to distinguish this little work with the name of a **Nursery** <note>original: "Seminarii," a term Comenius uses to describe a seedbed or foundation for learning</note>, in which there is equal care for both Things and Language. This was earnestly sought: that the confused chaos of things might receive some light of distinction in the eyes of beginners in wisdom, and that certain roots might be laid down for an infinite heap of words and phrases. In this way, the first and fundamental concepts of all Learning, Morality, and Piety might be formed. This, I say, was the goal; I am so far from boasting of having reached it that I am the first to recognize and confess its defects. However, Horace <note>A famous Roman poet (65–8 BCE)</note> gives hope of pardon among the wise, suggesting that in a great work (and even in a small one, full of trifles), it is permissible for sleep to creep in <note>original: "fas esse obrepere somnum," a reference to Horace’s "Ars Poetica," where he suggests that even the best writers (like Homer) occasionally nod off or make mistakes in a long work.</note>. And indeed, what has ever blossomed and ripened at the same time?*

*For this reason, we wish the printers to be requested and warned: if anyone desires to reprint this little book, they should not presume to do so without consulting the authors. For we hope that this small work will soon be rendered more polished and, with those things added which we have hinted at, will come forth more refined.*

*Meanwhile, I wish that some exceptionally learned person, powerful in the Latin tongue, might be persuaded to treat these same materials more fully using this same or a similar method. I hope they would choose to teach how to speak everything not only properly, but elegantly and vigorously, using the phrases of the classical authors! Thus it would come to pass that studious youth would possess a most pleasant **Garden** <note>original: "Viridarium," literally a plantation or pleasure garden</note> of universal things and pure Latinity, and a collected **Treasury** <note>original: "Thesaurum"</note> of the most precious scholarly learning.*

*May God grant that we all may dare something out of zeal for the public good!*
*Written in exile, March 4th, 1631.*

->J.A. Comenius.<-

## TO THE READER.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'T' within a square frame featuring a foliate design.</image-desc>
<margin>Hippocrates <note>The author references the famous Greek physician’s aphorism: "Life is short, art is long."</note></margin>
The term of life is *short*, the way to *art* is *long*: yet as *sin* and *disorder* may help to shorten that *vital* thread, which nature (left to herself) would spin out to a farther length: so *ignorance* and *folly* do help to *lengthen* that way to art, which wisdom and method might make far more compendious. No marvel then, if our progress be so slow, when we toil so much to remove or overleap those blocks, which we ourselves have laid in our own path. No marvel if it be so long before we can reach the *pith* of matter, when so much time is misspent in the *bark* of words: yea when the only study of the *Latin* tongue (whose highest preferment is, to be but the *Muses’* <term>trunchman</term> <note>An archaic term for an interpreter or spokesperson.</note>, and the common carrier between the learned) drains up above a quarter of a competent age: and if so large a space be wasted in the imitation of a mere *verbalist* <note>Someone focused entirely on words and grammar.</note>: how many ages will be requisite to the *perfection* of a *realist* <note>In this context, a "realist" is a student of "real things"—the sciences and the natural world—rather than just language.</note>.
<margin>Scaliger, Lipsius, Drusius, etc. <note>These were prominent 16th and 17th-century scholars and linguists.</note></margin>
Some indeed there have been of a more heroical strain, who striving to <term>gain-cope</term> <note>To encounter or overcome.</note> these <term>ambages</term> <note>Circuitous or winding paths; wordy obscurities.</note> by venturing on a new discovery, have happily made their voyage in half the time. The reasons, why we "with great effort produce great trifles" <note>original: "magno conatu magnas agere nugas"</note>, still bewilder ourselves in our own mazes, and plod on in the beaten road with so small success, may all be reduced to this one; in that we take such pleasure "to learn such things as should be unlearned" <note>original: "discere dediscenda"</note>, or such as are not worth the learning, but must be unlearned again: much like the *mystery* of *compliments*, the courting language, and other fooleries, which our gallants must needs in any case learn to practice when they are young and vain, and after learn to laugh at, if ever they grow grave and wise. 1. ## TO THE READER.

Great diligence is used to wean the student from the true, ancient, and genuine sound of the language (which would be much easier to learn) and to habituate him to a new, barbarous, Gothic pronunciation, which is far more intricate and difficult. For, not even mentioning the confusion of **vowels**, whose length—whether long or short—any <term>cobbler</term><note>Meaning a common, uneducated person.</note> could once better discern simply by hearing the word spoken than we can now with all our complex rules of **prosody** <note>The study of poetic meter and the patterns of sounds in language.</note>; it is certain that <term>Tully</term><note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the famous Roman orator.</note> and those of his age, when this language flourished in its prime and purity, never sounded the letter *c* as anything but the Greek *k* [kappa],

2. After the difficulty <margin>* Stephen Gardiner, etc.</margin> of *reading*, what greater *hindrance* than the affected perplexity of grammatical rules? Now, surely it was a merry world when the *Friars* ruled the roast, who ran mad upon this humor, and would never stop *rhyming* without all *reason*, insomuch that religion itself was turned to a matter of *rhyme*.

But the *ornament* of *meter* hath often corrupted the *plain-song* <note>The author uses a musical metaphor: "plain-song" is the simple, foundational melody of a chant, representing basic truth, while "descant" or meter is the complex ornamentation added on top.</note> of truth: for as this dotage blunted the edge of *devotion*, by tickling the ear and robbing the understanding; so it hindered the course of *learning*, by stuffing the precepts of arts (which for children, especially those who are unacquainted with the laws of versifying, cannot be too *plain, short, and orderly*) with much obscurity and confusion, many repetitions, and some gross falsehoods. 

Indeed, when the *intellectual* part hath fed upon a clear and distinct notion, a verse is not unfit to strengthen the *memory* <note>original: "retentive faculty"</note>, and may serve sometimes to *bundle up* a confused heap of particulars into a portable pack: but to disguise the *principal rule* under the veil of poetry, is to teach them to *dance*, who as yet cannot *walk*; and proves (as painting on glass) a means to darken the sense and overcast the clearer light with a needless cloud: which either putteth both master and scholar to a double toil (in stripping the verse of its habit, and turning it first into prose, before it can be conceived) or doth but quicken the memory (in a preposterous manner) to patter over some words by rote without understanding; and yet cumbers it as much by interspersing a multitude of *irrelevant details*, which (were it not to patch up a tattered verse) might well be spared.

# To the Reader.

The result is that since the common path is so tedious and tiresome before a student can be **enrolled** <note>original: "matriculated"</note> among those with a basic knowledge of **Latin**, it is therefore the quicker and wiser way to sail by **compass**, rather than to wander at **random**: to take a shorter and nearer route by the help of some abstract, which may be a **summary of the entire Latin language** <note>original: "epitome totius Latinismi"</note>, than to travel through so many volumes for **no other purpose but to learn Latin**. It is better to study the world in a **map** and measure its parts by a scale, rather than to cross the equator by sea and encircle the globe by navigation, **only** to know the circumference of the earth and the location of different climates. It is better to view all creatures in **Noah's Ark**, where they are shut up in pairs and confined to a narrow space, than to wander from land to land until a man happens upon one here and another there by chance, merely out of a desire to see them all. 

The best attempt yet available to make this project possible is this **Gate** <note>original: "Janua." Referring to Comenius's famous textbook, "Janua Linguarum Reserata" (The Door of Languages Unlocked).</note> of **J.A. Comenius**, in which:

1. All **root** <note>original: "primitive"</note> words, together with the chief and most common derivatives and compounds that make up the body of the **Latin tongue**, are so applied to their proper subject for which they were intended, that the **subject matter** helps to fix the **word** in the mind, and the word helps clarify the matter. For this purpose, opposites are so linked and set against each other in the same sentence that the one serves to clear the natural sense of the other. 

2. Great care is taken to use **words in their original, primary meaning** (which, being well understood, allows the other **borrowed** and **figurative** <note>original: "tropicall," from "trope," a figure of speech.</note> meanings to be easily recognized) unless where the proper sense has become obsolete and the metaphorical sense is more common. I mean such **words** as are in **common use**; and I call that the **proper sense** which either appears by a clear **etymology** <note>The study of word origins.</note> (breaking the word down into its original parts, as they lie unformed and newly hatched in the **nest**) or which is **most** frequently used by the learned. 

But where the word is of rarer use, or the origin is very questionable, or the thing itself is obscure or of lesser importance, there to demand exactness and correctness—or to not dare to apply to matters of our age such ancient terms as come closest to them, even if they do not fit exactly <note>original: "hit nor pat." An archaic idiom meaning to strike the mark or fit perfectly.</note> (and which, otherwise,

<meta>This page continues the translator's preface, shifting from the structural arrangement of the Latin sentences to the specific philosophy behind the English translation. The previous page discussed how the text was organized to help students learn grammar through context; here, the author explains why he has avoided a literal, word-for-word translation in favor of natural English expression.</meta>

### To the Reader.

The translation strives not to render the Latin **word-for-word** <note>original: *ad verbi* (likely *ad verbum*)</note> (a task better left to the teacher’s care and the student’s hard work) but truly to express the author’s meaning in such appropriate words and current phrases as an **Englishman** would recognize as his own. Therefore, in some places, I have ventured to change the **Latin** (even though it was perfectly fine before) only to make it comply better with good **English**. I have done this for three reasons:

**First**, for the benefit of foreigners. Just as the original text helps one attain **Latin**, foreigners who wish to learn our language may find the same help in this translation—namely, all our most common **English idioms** <note>original: "anglicisms"</note> and the main body of our tongue contained within the small size of this little book.

**Second**, to accustom a young student early on to a proper **English** style. This is far more difficult than to inflate an affected style with flashy foreign phrases or make it strut with pompous, nonsensical language <note>The original uses "bombast" and "fustian," terms for overwritten, padded, or pretentious speech.</note>. It is sheer folly to be curious and expert in foreign skills while remaining a stranger **at home**. It should be the care of every teacher to accustom a child early to the practice of good **English** as much as good **Latin**. Our **mother-tongue** is likely to be the most useful in practice; it is certainly as capable of scholarly expression and as adaptable to any kind of elegance as any other language.

**Third**, to guide a student toward a more ready expression of proper **Latin**. For a student who, in interpreting an author, works only **† word-for-word** <note>original: *verbatim*</note> and forces his own tongue 

<margin>† See *The English-Latin Hermes* <note>original: *Hermes Anglo-Latinus*, a contemporary grammar book.</note>.</margin>

to match the **Latin**—so that his very **English** is nothing but **Latin phrasing** <note>original: "Latinism"</note> in English words—will find himself at a loss later. When he encounters the same meaning in more natural **English** and must turn it back into **Latin**, even if he knows the right word to use, he will be as lost as if he had never seen it before, simply because he never encountered it in that "English habit" <note>Meaning he hasn't seen the word used in a natural English context.</note>, but only in a clumsier form. However, he who observes the unique idioms of both languages takes the right course to be exact in the usage of both. 

**English** terms that sound close to the **Latin** are 

<margin>* Except for those terms commonly used in a sense very different from their own original root.</margin>

purposely set aside **\*** so that there might be room for other more appropriate and native words. This is because the **Latin** itself, once known, will soon suggest such "false" **English** to a man—words that (like a **Jesuit**) strut in a new **English** outfit but are, in substance, **Roman** <note>The translator is using a religious metaphor common in the 17th century: just as Jesuits were viewed as foreign agents disguised in English clothes, "Latinate" English words might look English but follow foreign rules of logic. He prefers "home-bred" Anglo-Saxon words.</note>. Words enclosed in two semi-

### To the Reader.

Square brackets [ ] (whether in the original or the translation) signify synonyms for the preceding word and may be used interchangeably with the same meaning.

With these basic principles being thus established, the benefit that may arise for the advancement of youth and the prevention of much unnecessary trouble is left to the testimony of those who have had experience, and the trial of those who will put it into use <note>original: "put it in ure"</note>. I do not doubt that the plan <note>original: "plot"</note> itself will thrive, having progressed this far, even if the current editors <note>original: "undertakers"</note> fail to achieve full perfection. Every man is free to dislike whatever he pleases, provided that he himself produces some method which, with a high degree of reason, may better contribute to the public good.

->JOHN ROBOTHAM<-

***

*It is considered most appropriate to print the* Latin *entirely by itself, and the* English *following it, so that those who wish may have each bound separately. In this way, the translation may be more useful to the learner than if it stood (as it did before) right alongside the original, acting as a constant prompter close at hand.*

*The* Entrance <note>original: *Vestibulum*, the introductory work to Comenius's language system</note>, *which was previously attached as a preface to the* Gate of Languages <note>original: *Janua*</note>, *will soon be published on its own. It is a more suitable book than any currently available to serve as an introductory primer* <note>original: *Pueriles*, likely referring to the *Sententiae Pueriles*, a standard elementary Latin reader of the era</note> *to initiate a child into* Latin.

## Upon the Gate of the most learned and accomplished Man, J.A.
# COMENIUS.

*Throw open the gates, and unbar your doors, O Gate of Helicon* <note>original: "Heliconia Janua"; Helicon was the mountain home of the Muses</note>; *open the doors, O Forerunner of the Muses* <note>original: "Pieridum Prodroma"</note>.
*Whoever desires to surpass the peaks of the twin-forked hill* <note>The "bifidi clivi" refers to Mount Parnassus, the home of poetry and learning</note>,
*Will travel with you as a guide, where the straight path lies open.*
*As for him who delights to wander in the mazes of those who stray; let the devious error*
*Of a doubtful path lead him on:*
*Let Sisyphus* <note>A figure from myth condemned to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity</note> *pile up his cycles, and roll back those same*
*Rocks, and let him be the cause of his own delay.*
*But the studious troop shall seek the goal through new shortcuts,*
*Under your guidance, by a simpler method of study.*
*Approach with joy, beginner* <note>original: "Tyro," a term for a novice or recruit</note>, *and take the kernel from the shell:*
*Let both the tongue and the mind begin their proper work.*
*The mind takes up various matters, the nourishment due to it:*
*Through chosen words, pure speech shines forth.*
*There is no need to visit the Italian hills* <note>original: "Oenotrios colles"</note> *with a weary foot:*
*Traverse the land of the Latins* <note>original: "Latium," the region of Rome</note> *here, and hasten your journey.*
*This chest shall give to you the courses of the Roman tongue:*
*A tiny box unfolds the riches of Attalus* <note>Attalus was a King of Pergamum famous for his immense wealth</note>.
*Nor does reheated cabbage* <note>original: "crambe repetita," a Roman idiom for a boring, repetitive thing</note> *cloy the palate when served again:*
*Every comma will set forth a variety of feasts.*
*May the field of Comenius overflow with many-fold seeds,*
*And ever take pride in a similar harvest:*
*A rich and fertile soil, which blesses the prayers of the skillful farmer*
*With a constant abundance of crops:*
*A happy genius: under whose Presidency, learned Apollo*
*Gathers the sacred choir of Thespia* <note>The Muses</note> *into a narrow space.*
*This word-crafting machine* <note>original: "logodædala machina"</note> *boasts of you as its Vitruvius* <note>The famous Roman architect; the author is calling Comenius the architect of this language system</note>:
*Behold, a singer of the opening song* <note>original: "Parôdus"</note> *stands by as a helping craftsman.*
*Take this small effort, I pray, in good part, and do not disdain it:*
*It remains submissive to your directions.*
*Where it is permitted, we follow the Author’s footsteps closely,*
*And with you leading the way, we climb the mountain of the Muses* <note>original: "Aonidum jugum"</note>.

### CHAPTER I. *The Entrance.*

<margin>A greeting at the entrance.</margin>
1 <sup>a</sup> Greetings, friendly reader.
<margin>As things differ from one another.</margin>
2 If you ask what it means to be learned <note>original: "eruditum"; a term implying being well-taught or polished</note>; here is your answer: first, to have recognized <sup>b</sup> the differences between things, and to be able to designate each one by its proper name.
3. Is there nothing else besides? Truly, nothing at all.
4. He has laid the foundations of all learning and scholarship who has thoroughly learned the nomenclature <note>original: "nomenclaturam"; the system of names or terms used in a particular subject</note> of nature and art.
5. But perhaps that is difficult.
6. It is, if you do it against your will, or if you terrify yourself with a preconceived opinion.
7. After all, if there is to be any bitterness <note>original: "asperitatis"; meaning harshness or roughness</note>, it will be at the beginning.
<margin>at first sight, or on the face of it.</margin>
8. Do not the strokes of letters also seem like strange monsters to children <sup>*</sup> <note>The Latin "puellis" specifically refers to girls, but in this context of early education, it often implies young children generally.</note> at first glance?
9. But once they have applied a little effort, they perceive it to be child's play <note>original: "lusum"; a game or sport</note>.
10. The same happens in every matter: it appears laborious in its outward appearance.
11. But if you approach it, there is nothing that does not yield and submit itself even to a moderate talent.
12. He who desires, grasps everything; even those things which at the first attempt exceed his understanding.
<margin>we are urged to proceed.</margin>
13. <sup>a</sup> Come now then, whoever you are, I bid you to hope, and I forbid you to despair.
14. Look, see this small little work.
15. Here, however, as if in a summary <note>original: "breviario"; an abridgment or handbook</note>, the whole wor—

## CHAPTER 2. *Of the origin of the world.*

18. God created all things from nothing.
19. In the beginning, he spread out the vastest space (where heaven and earth exist).
20. And he filled it with a certain dark and formless mist.
21. From which, as if from matter, he shaped bodily creatures, distinguished by forms and various *accidental coverings* <term>original: "vestibus accidentibus"; in Scholastic philosophy, "accidents" are properties like color or size that are not part of an object's essential nature</term>, just as he had conceived the idea of each within himself.
22. And he implanted in each its own Nature, that is, the power of observing its own manner and kind and assigned place.

## CHAPTER 3. *Of the elements.*

23. Before all things indeed, he separated that confused Chaos into four species, according to degrees of density and rarity.
24. The thinnest and most subtle part he made bright and hot, and called it fire or light.
25. Another part, again thin, transparent, and lukewarm, he called air.
26. The third portion, fluid and cold, was Water:
27. Beneath which remained a thick sediment, Mud, or earth.
28. And these are simple bodies, from which composite [mixed] things arise.
29. For all other things consist of these.
30. Since they are generated from them, they are nourished by them, and they are resolved back into the same when they are corrupted <note>original: "corrumpuntur"; meaning to decay or break down into component parts</note>.

### CHAPTER 5. Concerning fire.

44. A fire arises from any spark, if you allow it.
<margin>Turf, mineral <insert>coal</insert>, ashes, stone-coals, or any kind of kindling <note>original: "fomes"</note>.</margin>

47. 65. From veins of water, gushing springs leap forth, from which brooks flow.

66. From the gathering of these, streams are formed, and finally large rivers, running continually within their banks until they empty themselves through their mouths [ *estuaries* ] into the sea: but if they overflow [ *exceed* ] their channels in a flood, the surrounding fields become stagnant.

69. Torrents are rainwater flowing down rapidly, from which overflows and floods arise.

71. If you sink anything in it, it will emerge: but what (after all) does it matter if clear water is muddied?

72. A bubble is made by a dripping drop.

### CAP. 8. Concerning the earth.

77. The **earth’s** surface is in some places wet, boggy, well-watered, or grassy; in others dry, parched, stony, or rugged.

<margin>a A Field.</margin>
78. In some places a <gloss>a</gloss> level plain extends far and wide; in others, mountains and valleys and hollows are seen: here mounds rise slightly; there lower-lying places, chasms, caves, and caverns sink down.

<margin>b A summit. * For those descending from the brow through the ridge [the side] to the roots of the mountain.</margin>
79. Hills and slopes are steep for those going toward the <gloss>b</gloss> peak, but sloping downward behind them *.

80. An earthquake is caused by underground blasts: if these burst out, landslides occur.

81. If you rub and crumble a clod of earth, it is dust; if you soak it, it is mud.

---

### CAP. 9. Concerning stones.

82. A **stone** crushed small is sand, which if it is coarser, is called grit and gravel.

83. Rocks lie on the ground (whether they stick out or are hidden): crags stand out.

<margin>c A pebble.</margin>
84. A <gloss>c</gloss> small stone having slipped into a shoe, unless it is removed, pinches.

<margin>* Hand-held, or rotating [turning.] d Whose edge is blunted.</margin>
85. With a whetstone * we sharpen <gloss>d</gloss> dull tools; with a flint we strike out fire; with a Lydian stone <note>A "touchstone" used to test the purity of gold and silver</note> we test metals, whether they be genuine or counterfeit.

86. Tufa is sandy and rough.

<margin>e Parian stone <note>A fine white marble from the Greek island of Paros, highly prized by ancient sculptors</note>.</margin>
87. Alabaster, a very white <gloss>e</gloss> marble, is cut out from a quarry.

88. The magnet turns itself directly to the north, turned entirely away from the south.

89. The most precious of gems is the carbuncle <note>Historically, any red gemstone that glows like a coal, usually a garnet or ruby</note>, the second after that is the Diamond, then the Ruby, Sapphire, Emerald, Jasper etc., which shine with many facets.

90. Hematite [bloodstone], the Cock-stone, and the Toad-stone are of inferior quality <note>original: "Alectorius, Bufonius"; these were "fabulous stones" believed to be found inside animals—the former in a rooster’s gizzard and the latter in a toad’s head—and were worn as protective amulets</note>.

91. Large pearls are found in shells.

<margin>* Which resemble a bush turning into stone.</margin>
92. Corals are the small branches of a sea-shrub *.

93. Glass has the appearance of crystal, but not the hardness: it is cut with emery <note>original: "smyrite," a very hard mineral powder used for grinding and cutting</note>.

### CHAP. 10. Concerning metals.

94. Metals are dug out [excavated] from mines; from these, because they both melt and harden [become solid], various things are forged.

<margin>† Because of the most excellent mixing of its elements.</margin>
95. Gold is the most perfect, because it is the purest and heaviest, especially <gloss>2</gloss> refined gold <note>original: "obryzum" — pure gold that has been tested by fire</note>.

96. Even if you put it into a furnace a hundred times, it loses not the smallest bit of its substance.

<margin>
<gloss>a</gloss> Refined.
* Made into vessels and engraved [raw, not yet carved].
</margin>
97. Silver * comes closest to this when it is pure and unmixed; but it has dross <note>original: "scorias" — the waste material or scum removed during smelting</note>, which is burned away.

98. Iron, however hard it may be, is eaten away by rust: when it is hardened multiple times, it is called steel.

<margin><gloss>b</gloss> To Cyprian bronze <note>Copper was famously associated with the island of Cyprus, from which its name is derived</note>.</margin>
99. <insert>b</insert> Verdigris <note>The green crust or pigment formed by the oxidation of copper</note> clings to copper. From bell-metal, brass-founders cast bells.

100. Brass is bronze colored with calamine <note>original: "cadmiâ" — a zinc-rich mineral used in the ancient process of making brass</note>: it can only be cast [it is meltable, not hammerable] because of its brittleness.

101. Tin is softer and cheaper than amber or jet, and lead is softer and cheaper than this.

102. Nothing is more marvelous than quicksilver [mercury]: it is liquid, yet not wet [it does not soak].

<margin><gloss>1</gloss> You dip it.</margin>
103. For whether you pour it over something, or <gloss>1</gloss> dip something into it, or sprinkle it, it wets nothing.

<margin>
* A certain saltiness of the earth, or a salty sweat.
† Because it is sticky and becomes gummy, and because of its stickiness does not easily break apart.
<gloss>°</gloss> Made from burnt ochre.
* For besides salt that is boiled down or thickens in lakes, there is also rock salt, dug out from a mine.
</margin>
104. Salt, alum *, vitriol [copperas], saltpeter, sulfur, bitumen †, naphtha, white lead, red lead, chalk, <gloss>°</gloss> red earth, cinnabar, etc., are called mineral juices *.

### CHAP. 11. Concerning trees and fruits.

105. A plant grows by drinking in moisture through the fibers of its roots.

106. Deprived of this, it wilts, withers, and dries up.

107. It is called a stalk or stem, as far as it spreads itself into branches, twigs, and foliage.

108. When these are gone, it has the name of a trunk, a log, or a stump.

<margin>* Which can be stripped of its bark.</margin>
109. On the outside is the bark *, inside are the inner layers <note>original: "Libri" — the thin membranes between the bark and wood; in antiquity, these were used as writing surfaces, giving us the Latin word for "book"</note> (which, while green, can be peeled); the pith is in the innermost part.

110. Leaves fall from trees and grow back; except for evergreen trees <note>original: "gummosis" — resinous trees</note>, which are green continually [on and on], such as the boxwood, the yew, etc.

<margin>$\dagger$ In Latin, a tree name most often ends in *-us*; its fruit in *-um*; and the place where it is planted in *-etum*. For example, a cherry-tree (*cerasus*) in a cherry-orchard (*cerasetum*) bears cherries (*cerasa*); ash-trees grow in an ash-grove.</margin>
111. Fruit trees $\dagger$ [apple-trees], citron-trees [citron-apples], pear-trees, fig-trees, and olive-trees are cultivated: the ash, beech, alder, and mountain ash are wild; as are the wild pine, wild pear, wild olive, etc.

112. All the former are fruit-bearing: most of the latter are sterile [barren], such as the birch, white poplar, and black poplar.

113. Some are shade-bearing: specifically, the lime-tree [linden], the plane-tree, the elm, and other broad-leaved trees.

<margin>\* It is called *oleocarpos* <note>original: "oleocarpos" — from Greek, meaning 'oil-fruited'</note>, because it sheds its flower before the seed has ripened.</margin>

<margin>$\dagger$ From which exudes the "fir-tear" [Venetian turpentine].</margin>
115. The fir-tree $\dagger$ is tall, as are the pitch-pine, the larch, the cypress, and the cedar.

<margin>\* The mulberry-tree buds last of all once the cold has passed, and it is among the last to lose its leaves; therefore, it is imagined to be the wisest of trees <note>This was a common ancient belief recorded by Pliny the Elder</note>.</margin>
116. The palm tree bears dates [large dates] and the more heavily it is pressed down and curved, the more strongly it strives upward; hence it is used as a symbol of victory \*.

<margin>b The calyx [bud-casing].</margin>
<margin>$\dagger$ "Falling" means fleeting [not at all durable].</margin>

119. The cherry hangs from a long ^o stalk, the sour cherry from a rather short one.

### CHAPTER 14. On Animals, and first of Birds.

142. Whatever is endowed with life, sense, and motion, is an animal.

143. For birds <note>original: "alites" — large-winged or omen-bearing birds</note> fly, water-creatures swim (the former with feathers, the latter with fins), four-footed animals run, and reptiles creep.

144. Fliers are two-footed (they say the Bird of Paradise <note>original: "Manucodiatam" — from the Malay 'manuk dewata', birds of the gods; it was a common myth that they lacked feet and lived entirely in the air</note> is footless) and feathered and beaked (except the bat, which is hairy and toothed).

145. Gathering grains one by one with their beak, they fill their crop: none of them urinate <note>Comenius notes that birds lack a urinary bladder and excrete waste in a single form</note>.

### CHAP. 15. Concerning aquatic creatures.

163. Fish eject the water they have taken into their mouths through their gills <note>original: "branchias"</note>.

164. The scaly ones are viviparous <gloss>bringing forth live young</gloss>, the smooth ones are oviparous <gloss>egg-laying</gloss> <note>Comenius here follows an older, incorrect biological classification; most scaly fish are actually egg-layers.</note>.

165. Of these, the males have milt <gloss>soft roe</gloss>, and the females have eggs <gloss>hard roe</gloss>.

166. River fish include the sturgeon [royal fish], the pike-perch <note>original: "Amia exox"</note>, the slippery eel (which, if you try to grab it, slips away), the bullhead, the mullet, the barbel, the [golden] trout, the gray mullet, the bleak, the gudgeon [bottom-dweller], the eelpout, and the minnow.

167. Pond fish include the carp [cyprid], the pike [water-wolf], the perch, the tench, the saddled bream, the green-fish, and the red-fish.

<margin>† Mackerel, turbot, sardine, cuttlefish, seal.</margin>
168. Sea fish: the salmon, the moray eel, the conger eel, the ray, oysters, and various sea-monsters.

169. They bring to us salted and preserved herrings in barrels, but dried ones—as well as sun-toasted flatfish <note>original: "passeres", here referring to plaice or flounder rather than sparrows</note>—in bundles.

170. Dried cod <note>original: "Asellus arefactus", also known as stockfish</note> is not fit for eating unless it is thoroughly beaten.

171. The dolphin surpasses all in speed, and the whale <note>original: "balæna [cetus]"</note> in size.

<margin>a Sucking-cups <note>original: "Acetabulis"</note>.</margin>
172. The crab and the lobster [crayfish, sea-locust] walk forward and backward with their claws<sup>a</sup>.

### CHAPTER 19. On Insects.

217. Insects are, first of all, various worms: among which earthworms gnaw at dung-heaps, wood-borers <note>original: "cossi", likely referring to the larvae of the goat moth</note> gnaw wood, moths gnaw books, vine-fretters <note>original: "volvoces", a type of caterpillar or beetle that rolls leaves</note> gnaw vines, weevils gnaw grain, and mites gnaw cheeses.

<margin>a Crab-shaped.</margin>
218. Nits, lice, crab-lice, **a** fleas, gnats, bedbugs, mites, and intestinal worms infest us; as do ticks and leeches [bloodsuckers].

<margin>b Those making a buzzing sound.</margin>
219. Silkworms produce silk [raw silk], buzzing **b** bees make hexagonal honeycombs of honey (on which the drones feed); sending out a swarm as if they were establishing a new colony.

220. Hornets and wasps have a sharper sting than bumblebees.

221. Cattle, when stung by a gadfly <note>original: "oestro", "tabano", or "asilo", all referring to stinging flies that drive livestock into a frenzy</note>, jump about.

<margin>† There is also the mayfly.</margin>
222. There are many kinds of beetles and locusts: some are edible †.

<margin>* Or cockchafers, golden beetles. d The earwig, the little shears, the biter. e The stroller. f The glow-worm, the firefly.</margin>
223. Cankerworms * and beetles, blistering beetles, red beetles, and horned beetles, moths [fire-moths], fireflies [glow-worms], etc. are flying insects: the mill-beetle **d**, the centipede [hundred-legs, many-legs **e**], the woodlouse, the sow-bug [little donkey], the crane-fly, the cockchafer, and the glow-worm [night-light **f**] crawl.

<margin>g The fire-moth.</margin>
224. The cicada, springing from cuckoo-spit <note>original: "cuculi saliva"; a reference to the foam produced by spittlebug nymphs, which was historically believed to be cuckoo spit</note>, chirps outdoors, while the cricket **g** does so at home.

225. The ant is tiny but busy, always carrying straws and crumbs.

<margin>h The chrysalis.</margin>
226. The spider weaves a checkered web. A caterpillar, wasting away and lifeless, is called a chrysalis **h**; revived, it becomes a butterfly.

### CHAPTER 22. Concerning the internal organs.

**266.** Come now, let us look at the **internal organs** <note>original: "viscera", referring to the soft organs of the body cavities</note>.
<margin>* Of which the last two or three are called **wisdom teeth** <note>original: "genuini" or "sophronisteres"</note> because they are born late, around the twenty-eighth year.</margin>
<margin>† With the **pylorus** <note>the opening from the stomach to the intestine</note> tightly shut.</margin>
**267.** **Food** is cut by the **front teeth** <gloss>incisors or "smiling" teeth</gloss> or the **canine teeth**, and chewed by the **molars** * (for the **mouth** <note>original: "bucca", referring to the cheek or mouth cavity</note> is a mill); it is sent down through the **throat** <gloss>esophagus</gloss> to the **stomach** (in four-legged animals first to the **rumen**, then to the **omasum**, then to the **abomasum** <note>original: "pances"</note>, and finally the true stomach called the **reticulum** <note>original: "echinus"</note>), and is squeezed and narrowed † <gloss>constricted</gloss> above and below. There, with everything crushed and thoroughly mixed, it is softened by the first digestion and processed into **chyle** <gloss>into a kind of cream-like appearance</gloss>.
<margin>* **Duodenum**, **jejunum**, **ileum** <note>the three parts of the small intestine</note>.</margin>
<margin>† **Caecum**, **colon**, **rectum**, all of which have one passage but not the same width.</margin>
<margin>* Like the **Esquiline gate** <note>an ancient Roman gate associated with the disposal of waste</note>. ᵃ The **urine channels**.</margin>
**268.** When it is thus prepared, and passed through the now relaxed **pylorus** into the **thinner intestines** *, the **mesenteric veins** <note>original: "venæ meseraïcæ"</note> suck it out and draw it forth; they carry it away—separated from the coarser excrements (which are cast out through the **thicker intestines** † and the **anus** <gloss>bottom</gloss> * as dung, filth, and ordure)—to the **liver** (and by the same action they return blood to the intestines), where a separation happens once more.
**269.** The **watery part** <note>original: "serosum"</note> goes to the **kidneys** (through which it is strained as if through a sieve) and from there is dripped through the **ureters** ᵃ into the **bladder**, becoming **urine** <gloss>liquid waste</gloss> which is discharged by urinating.
**270.** The richer part receives a red color from the liver and becomes **humor** <note>original: "chymus"</note> and **blood**; this is distributed through the **veins**, and like a thickening dew it clings and sticks to every part until it is everywhere assimilated <gloss>integrated into its very substance</gloss>.
**271.** Meanwhile, the **spleen** <gloss>the spleen</gloss> attracts and again expels **melancholy** <note>black bile, believed to be a bodily humor</note>; the **gallbladder** <gloss>the gall-bladder or gall-vessel</gloss> handles the **bile** <gloss>yellow bile</gloss>.

**272.** Phlegm [mucus] flows through all parts. The glands are cleaning organs <note>original: "emunctoria", referring to organs that filter or purge fluids</note> through which excess moisture passes out.

**274.** By this heat, it beats without rest and produces the vital spirit, which it shares in every direction through the pulsing **arteries**.

</margin>

### CHAPTER 29. On the will and the emotions.

360. It is the nature of the **Will** to love and desire good things, and to hate and reject evil things.
361. It happens by accident if these things please someone and those displease: for in such cases, outward appearance deceives the will, causing it to choose the worse options or to scorn things of which it is ignorant.
362. See, however, how subject the will is to the emotions! How repeatedly it is disturbed by them!
<margin>* Longing for them makes one waste away.</margin>
363. Are good things absent? The will desires, wishes, and craves them*; it hopes for the best, pants after them, and tries and schemes however it can, yet nonetheless it fears frustration.
364. From this come desires, prayers, hope, zeal, undertakings, efforts, and anxiety.
365. Before it obtains what it seeks, it bears even the space of a short delay with weariness.
366. Are the good things present? The will is thrilled with eagerness, it rejoices, is glad, and leaps for joy; it delights itself in enjoying them, yet fears to lose them: hence come cheerfulness, gladness, and pleasure, yet always joined with fear.
367. Are they snatched away? It is saddened, it grieves, and it complains: hence come sadness, regret, complaining, and heartache.
368. But evil things disturb and distract the will even more.
369. For it abominates, turns away from, and avoids things to come; yet it dreads them, which causes it to tremble and be distressed: hence come aversion, fear and dread, trembling and anxiety.
370. As evils approach, it grows terrified, shudders, and trembles at them, or it is stunned and faint: hence come terror, horror, and trepidation.
371. When they have arrived, it is angry at the one who brought them; it mourns, deplores, and laments the things inflicted: hence come anger, sorrow, and mourning.
372. The will behaves differently regarding the good or evil of others.
373. In the former case, it congratulates or envies the fortunate; in the latter, it pities the unhappy, grieves for their lot, or (if the will is perverse) it exults.
374. Ignorance of the good brings neglect and contempt; its violation brings zeal; a surplus of it satisfies but also brings loathing.
375. It is shame and modesty if someone blushes because of base things:

## CHAPTER 31. On the cultivation of gardens.

<margin>† Whose guardian is the forest-keeper.</margin>
379. A garden is either an orchard, or a pleasure garden, or a park for animals or an oak grove†.
<margin>* By mounding the earth high.</margin>
380. It is enclosed either by a mound* or a wall (made of stone <gloss>cemented</gloss>, brick, or of clay and wickerwork), or by plants, or by a fence <gloss>enclosure</gloss> woven from stakes <gloss>poles</gloss>, poles, or other flexible twigs.
<margin>* Such as a ditcher or one who prepares the ground for vines.</margin>
<margin>a With a hoe or a weeding hook.</margin>
381. The gardener <gloss>vegetable grower</gloss> digs* with a mattock, a hoe, a shovel <gloss>spade</gloss>, and a trenching tool; he scatters seeds through the garden beds <gloss>small plots</gloss>, and weeds out stray plants a with a weeding-plane, or uproots them <gloss>plucks them out by the roots</gloss>.
382. The tree-dresser, having planted the nursery with cuttings or quicksets (it is neat and elegant if they are arranged in a quincunx <note>A pattern of five points, like the dots on a die; Comenius suggests this geometric arrangement for both aesthetic beauty and efficient use of space.</note>), grafts shoots onto the cuttings, waters the grafted plants, prunes the buds and overgrown twigs with a pruning-knife, cuts off suckers, and arches flexible and compliant shrubs into a topiary scene.
383. Oil is pressed from olives: the dregs settle at the bottom, and the olive-husks are thrown away.
384. The beekeeper tends the hives and melts the wax.

[3]86. One to whom lands and leased estates are let for a set time for a certain fee is a **contractor** <note>original: *manceps*</note>: one to whom a farmhouse <note>original: *villa*</note> is entrusted is a **steward** and a **tenant farmer**. A **sharecropper** <note>original: *colonus partiarius*</note> divides the fruits of the land with the landlord.

<margin>a More fruitfully.</margin>
<margin>b Enriched with manure.</margin>
387. A field that has been worked and cleared of turf roots, so that it may be more fertile <sup>a</sup>, is fertilized <sup>b</sup> before sowing with dung or marl <note>a soil mixture of clay and lime used as fertilizer</note>.

388. Fallow land <note>original: *novale*</note>, land plowed for the first time <note>original: *vervactum*</note>, and a rested field is more productive after a break than land sown every year <note>original: *restibili*</note>; the latter, however fertile and rich, becomes barren [*becomes exhausted*] from frequent cultivation.

389. He who is about to plow joins oxen to the plow, not with ropes but with a yoke.

<margin>c Goading.</margin>
<margin>d Breaks up the soil.</margin>
<margin>e Ridges.</margin>
390. Then, driving and <sup>c</sup> urging them on with a goad, he plows <sup>d</sup>, repeats the plowing, plows a third time, sows, and harrows through the ridges <sup>e</sup> and turnings <note>the *versuras* or "turns" at the end of a field</note>.

391. While making ridges, he holds the plow-handle <note>original: *stiva*</note> with one hand (lest he wander from the line <note>original: *deliret*—the Latin origin of the word "delirious," meaning to wander from the furrow</note>) and the plow-staff <note>original: *ralla*</note> with the other; and the knife <note>the coulter</note> with the plowshare, fixed into the plow-beam, cuts the furrows until the acre <note>original: *jugerum*—the amount of land a yoke of oxen could plow in a day</note> is finished.

<margin>f Drainage channels, furrows for water.</margin>
392. A ridge <sup>f</sup> is made crosswise to drain away the moisture.

393. The harrow [*a heavy rake*] must be fitted with iron teeth in clayey soil; in sandy soil, a wooden one is enough.

<margin>g Inflict.</margin>
394. When the crops begin to sprout, there is a danger that a storm may bring <sup>g</sup> disaster; and so that the field does not grow wild with tares and cockle, or be choked by wild vetch, there is a need for weeding [*hoeing*].

<margin>h With a small hook or sickle.</margin>
395. When the harvest is ready, the reapers reap with a sickle <sup>h</sup> and arrange the stalks in handfuls.

396. Afterwards, they gather them into shocks <note>bundles of grain</note>, which they bind with straw ropes, while the stubble and gleanings are left in the field.

397. Then they carry them into the granaries on wagons, or pile them into heaps.

398. The threshers thresh and beat them out on the threshing floor with a flail (formerly they used a threshing sledge); the straw and chaff are left behind.

<margin>i For a while.</margin>
399. Then they toss it up for a little while <sup>i</sup> with a winnowing fan, so that the chaff may be separated.

400. If any dirt still remains, they sift it with a sieve so that it may be cleaned and become grain; which is then brought into the granaries, moved about with a shovel (lest it grow moldy), and leveled with a measuring rod once measured.

### CHAPTER 33. On Milling.

<margin>* From mixing and husking.</margin>
401. In ancient times, they only pounded and rubbed grain with pestles in a mortar; hence the name "peeled barley" <note>original: *ptisana*</note> was given.

402. Afterward, they crushed it with a rough pestle in a bakehouse; from this, porridges and spelt-grits were made.

<margin>a Hand-turned or tread-mills.</margin>
<margin>b Water mills.</margin>
403. Most recently, mills were invented (at first tread-mills <gloss>a</gloss>, then donkey-mills, then water-mills <gloss>b</gloss> and windmills [which have wings]).

<margin>c It is sifted.</margin>
404. There, the flour is ground by millstones (the upper stone <note>original: *catillo*</note> and the lower stone <note>original: *metâ*</note>), then sifted <gloss>c</gloss> through a hair-cloth bag and shaken out, with the bran scattered outside.

405. But he who grinds [the miller] gapes for gain <note>The author makes a pun on *molit* (he grinds) and *emolumento* (profit/gain).</note>.

### CHAPTER 36. On Butchery.

<margin>a Mutton.</margin>
**420.** The butcher <note>original: *lanio*</note> slaughters fat animals in the slaughterhouse—for lean, skinny ones killed by hunger are not edible <note>original: *vesca*</note>, and who would eat them?
