### CAP. 37. *On Hunting.*

423. **T**he hunter surrounds the thickets with a ring of nets <note>original: *indagine*</note>, lures wild beasts into pits and pitfalls, or tracks and hunts his prey by the scent of keen-scented dogs.

<margin>a Scent-hounds, or those that have a keen sense of smell. b French dogs <note>referring to Harriers or similar hounds</note>.</margin>
424. For those that hunt by scent <gloss>a</gloss> track them down; greyhounds and harriers <gloss>b</gloss> pursue and overtake them by their tracks. The shaggy water-dog dives; the spaniel <note>original: *hispaniolus*, literally "little Spaniard"</note> [used for hawking] flushes the covey of partridges and gives a sign by barking: all of these are hunting dogs.

425. **T**he doe, when she falls into the nets and various stretched snares, is entangled and killed; if she escapes, she hastens her flight.

<margin>* With teeth sticking out of the mouth.</margin>
426. **T**he foaming wild boar gnashes his teeth <gloss>*</gloss> and bristles his hair; but he is killed by being pierced through with a hunting-spear.

<margin>* or a wicker basket.</margin>

### CAP. 39. *On Bird-catching.*

428. **T**he bird-catcher <note>original: *auceps*, the root of "augury" and "aviation"</note>, having set up his fowling-place, either covers small birds with nets after they have been enticed and baited by decoys, or entangles them with lime-twigs <note>sticks coated in "birdlime," a sticky adhesive used to trap birds</note> (which he sets out on a perch or a long pole), or traps them in the snares of a springe, a trap, or a noose.

429. **T**hose to which he grants life, he imprisons in cages, either together or separately.

430. **I**f any bird, hindered by a shackle, frees [untangles] itself, it flies away, unless it entangles itself again in the snares.

### CAP. 41. On the Preparation of Drinks.

439. The vine-dresser plants young vines and propagates them by layers; he digs the vineyard with a two-pronged hoe; he supports the shoots with stakes or props; a little later he prunes the leaves, then harvests the grapes: the harvest being finished, he leaves the gleaning of the clusters for the poor.

<margin>
† Bound with willow hoops so that it does not leak.
</margin>
440. The vat presses the berry-filled grapes: from these being pressed, the wine-press squeezes out a sweet juice: which, transferred from the vat into a cask † or a jar, is called Must; and after it has been cleared of dregs, it is called wine, a drink suitable for cheering the sorrowful: especially if it is clarified by fire.

<margin>
c It will bear age <note>i.e., it will age well</note>.
</margin>
441. Year-old wine is best; this year's wine is somewhat dreggy; a noble wine, though old, c will remain strong; watered-down wine quickly turns sour and spoils.

442. Artificial wines are: wormwood wine, elecampane wine, honeyed wine, pear wine, etc.

<margin>
d It loses its taste <note>becomes insipid</note>.
</margin>
443. Boiled-down wine is new wine; spoiled wine is flat wine, <gloss>as it grows old d it turns flat.</gloss>

e Mead.
</margin>
<margin>
f Intoxicating.
</margin>
444. Where these are not abundant, mead e <gloss>honey-water</gloss> is brewed; and likewise beer, both small <note>meaning weak or light beer</note> and strong <gloss>pure or unmixed f</gloss>.

### CHAP. 42. On Horsemanship and Driving.

451. 452. The breast-band, the crupper <note>the strap passing under the horse's tail</note>, the saddle-cloth, and other trappings serve for its decoration.

453. A jolting horse shakes the rider; a pacer [an Asturconian horse <note>original: *asturco*, a breed known for a smooth gait</note>] walks gently at a trot, and does not stumble.

454. The driver yokes the extra horse to the saddle-horse, and drives the leader before him.

455. Great lords are carried in six-horse coaches, in state-carriages and covered wagons; commoners in four-horse, three-horse, or two-horse chariots; and that in a hired carriage or a two-wheeled cart [a four-wheeled wagon]; in some places even in a light chaise.

456. Loads are transported by wagon, heavy cart, and sledge; the sick by a stretcher-carriage; the delicate by a litter.

457. A chariot has wheels composed of a hub, twelve spokes, six felloes <note>original: *pfidibus*, likely a variation of *apsidibus*, the curved wooden sections of the rim</note>, and as many iron rims; but the axles—

### CHAP. 43. On Seafaring.

<margin>a So that they may import them.</margin>
462. Sailors, intending to bring exotic goods from across the sea <gloss>a</gloss>, board the ship and navigate the deep [crossing the sea].

<margin>a The steersman.</margin>
<margin>b They spread them out.</margin>

<margin>a If there is a calm, a state of stillness.</margin>

(However, the winds drive a swift boat [such as a light galley or skiff] more quickly than oars or tow-ropes can pull a trireme <gloss>b</gloss>). ### CHAP. 44. On Travel.

475. Let the traveler, proceeding toward his destination, go directly and by a shortcut without winding ways; let him not turn aside [divert] to byways.

<margin>a The main or public road.</margin>
476. Let him not desert the highway <gloss>a</gloss> for the sake of an unknown path, unless the track be well-worn and there is a skilled guide or companion for the journey.

477. He who fears trackless places and rugged roads should never go astray.

478. A fork in the road <note>original: *bivium*</note> is deceptive: therefore, so you do not wander, ask those you meet at the very parting of the way and the bend, which way should one go? This way or that? Should one turn to the right or to the left?

479. Winding paths and crossroads do not mislead in the same way.

480. So that you may travel abroad <note>original: *peregrinari*</note> without an interpreter, be skilled in the language.

<margin>† Those who drive up the price of grain and monopolists harm everyone through their monopolies.</margin>

## CHAPTER 46. Concerning the clothing trades.

<margin>a. In a pond.</margin>
497. Flax and hemp are soaked in a still $^a$ pond; once dried, they are crushed with a flax-brake, then carded, with the flock remaining there and the tow <note>original: *stupa* — the coarse, broken fibers of flax or hemp</note> here.

498. Then the spinners, having attached the task of wool to the distaff, draw out the threads, whether with a reel or with a spindle and whorl.

499. From the yarn-windle or the reel, the spun thread is wound into balls, from which the web <note>original: *tela* — the fabric on the loom</note> is made.

500. The weaver, weaving the woof [weft] into the warp with a shuttle, makes linen and fine cloth; so that it may become white, it is bleached in the sun.

501. Two-threaded cloth <note>original: *bilex*</note> requires a double leash <note>original: *licium* — the cords of a loom's harness</note>, three-threaded cloth requires a triple one.

502. Much the same is done in wool-working.

<margin>
* Once the fleece has been shorn [greasy wool.]
† The cloth-shearer polishes it, makes it combed, raises the nap, and shears the stuffing.
b. In a vat.
c. To a dull [color].
d. He measures out.
</margin>
503. Cotton [bumbast, wood-wool] or wool * is combed, carded, spun, woven, and the threads pass into cloth: which, if it is thin-woven, the fuller thickens <note>original: *constipat*</note>, stretches out with hooked nails, whitens, and cleans with fuller's earth †: The dyer [stainer] dyes it [infuses it] in a $^b$ vat, not with a thin [faint] vanishing, dull $^c$ color; but with one that is deep, lasting, lively, or twice-dyed <note>original: *dibapho* — a term for the highest quality cloth, literally "dipped twice"</note>.

504. The tailor [clothier] measures $^d$, cuts with shears, and sews garments with a needle and thimble (but takes care that the seams are not noticeable), and sometimes he even unsews the joints and unweaves the threads, and sews up the rips again, and folds it into pockets and pleats [grooves].

### CHAPTER 47. Types of Clothing.

<margin>* An ensemble of clothes.</margin>
509. Clothing, which was given to those cast out of Paradise to cover their nakedness, is foolishly used for the sake of pride.

510. As often as we put it on, take it off, or change it, it is a burden and a delay to us.

511. Some enjoy loose clothing, others tight, in various fashions. To dress in silk so thin that it is see-through is immodest; to strip oneself in public, or to dishonorably expose a part that should be covered, smacks of lewdness.

<margin>a. A doublet.</margin>
<margin>* Lined with underlying cloth; stuffed; supported by padding.</margin>
<margin>b. A short cloak.</margin>
<margin>† The Romans walked about in togas, but with bare shins, and often without shoes.</margin>
512. Men’s clothing includes: the $^a$ doublet with sleeves, the waistcoat <note>original: *colobium*, a short-sleeved or sleeveless tunic</note> lacking sleeves, breeches <note>original: *femoralia*</note>, the ankle-length gown, the cape, the military cloak $^b$, the heavy woollen cloak, and the general's robe †.

<margin>c. Eyelet-patterned or checkered.</margin>
<margin>* Veils, cheek-guards, a mantle, a forehead-band, a breast-piece, a hair-pin. A fan creates a little breeze for cooling. A parasol shades the face and protects against the harm of the sun.</margin>
513. Women’s clothing includes: the mantle, the gown, the linen smock, coifs <note>head coverings</note>, robes, aprons, the headband, the hair-net $^c$, and the headdress *.

<margin>d. Shin-bands or garters.</margin>
514. Common to both: the shirt, the under-shirt, the hood or collar, the cap (the top of which is the peak), the tiara or turban, tunics, gloves, stockings, garters $^d$, shoes (having soles, lacing, and thongs), slippers, sandals, cork-soled sandals, and buskins <note>original: *cothurni*, boots designed to fit either foot</note>.

<margin>e. Buttoned or buckled.</margin>
515. All these, where necessary, are fastened with pins, hooks, clasps, buckles, and buttons <note>original: *noduli*</note>, which are tied or joined with loops, eyelets, or small discs $^e$.

<margin>f. A belt or girdle.</margin>
<margin>* Tight or loose.</margin>
516. With a belt $^f$ we gird and ungird ourselves, and with laces we tie knots * tight or loosen them.

517. We wrap ourselves in cloaks, thick winter coats, and other such outer garments.

518. Embellishments and ornaments are added: small turbans, ribbons (with which curls and other things are bound), headbands, fringes, borders, dangling ribbons, and flaps.

<margin>† Hanging from the earlobe.</margin>
519. Also rings, neck-chains, necklaces, earrings †, bracelets, gold-leaf spangles, gilded studs, small pins, and so on: the works of the jewelers.

### CHAPTER 48. Concerning the Crafts of Artisans.

<margin>a. Heaped up from living turf.</margin>
522. Originally, caves and caverns, huts and leafy booths, little cottages made of sod <margin>a</margin> and small hovels <note>original: *gurgustiola*</note> were dwellings; now everything is filled with buildings—nay, even with mad constructions <note>The author implies that modern architecture is excessively grand or extravagant compared to ancient simplicity</note>.

523. These are sometimes low, sometimes lofty; two-storied or three-storied <note>original: *distega, tristega*</note> (having three or more floors), and they are either the inhabitant's own property, or rented and let for hire.

524. Who lives willingly in a meager cottage?

<margin>b. He constructs.</margin>
525. The architect, having first drawn a ground-plan <term>ichnography <note>a map of the floor or foundation</note></term> [or a profile sketch <note>original: *sciographia*</note>] of the whole structure, builds <margin>b</margin> according to that model <note>original: *hypotyposin*</note>; with the help of workmen performing their tasks with axe and hammer.

<margin>c. Sandy mortar.</margin>
<margin>d. A protective casing or brick-work layer.</margin>
526. The stonemason [or bricklayer] builds walls with rubble-stone (prepared by the stone-cutter) or fired brick and mortar <margin>c</margin> using a level and a plumb-line; he fills the gaps with packing-stones; using a trowel, he coats them <margin>d</margin> with plaster-work, namely wet lime (not quicklime) or gypsum.

<margin>e. Shavings and splinters.</margin>
<margin>f. Daubed with mud.</margin>
527. The carpenter <note>original: *lignarius faber*</note>, with a beam secured by iron clamps, hews it exactly with an adze—with chips and splinters <margin>e</margin> flying off—and cuts the knots <note>literally "calluses"</note> out of the wood; he drills and pierces it with an auger; he lifts things with pulleys; he arranges the partition walls, which are made of wattle-work <note>woven branches</note> and smeared <margin>f</margin> with mud mixed with chaff; he makes it firm by driving in nails.

<margin>g. Rot, lest it become decayed.</margin>
528. Let timber be felled after the full moon, so that the sapwood <margin>g</margin> does not suffer from decay.

<margin>h. Cleaves it apart.</margin>
<margin>i. Small dry twigs.</margin>
<margin>† He hedges in the cut-down coppice-wood so that it may grow back again.</margin>
529. The woodcutter fells trees and uproots them from the stump, then cuts the logs lying on the ground; he saws the heartwood with a saw (the sawdust falling away); he drives in a wedge with a mallet and splits <margin>h</margin> it; he piles up stacks and gathers bundles of brushwood <margin>i</margin> †.

<margin>k. A small hatchet or adze.</margin>
530. The cabinet-maker [or chest-maker] planes down planks and thin boards with a hatchet <margin>k</margin> or a plane, joins and fastens them together with tenons <note>tongue-and-groove joints</note>, glues them with glue, bonds them with solder <note>while *ferrumine* usually refers to metal, here it implies a permanent bond</note>, and coats them with varnish.

A house deeply founded, very well-timbered, skillfully built, fashioned with proper symmetry, well-solidified at the corners, and stabilized with columns *, lasts a very long time unharmed and well-maintained <note>original: *sarta-tecta* — an old legal phrase meaning "patched and roofed," or kept in good repair</note> <margin>q</margin>.

<margin>
q. Impervious to wind and the injuries of the weather.
r. A buttress, a prop, or a support.
</margin>
38. Therefore, it is necessary that a building which is tottering and leaning over [sinking] <margin>q</margin> be propped up with a pillar <margin>r</margin> or other supports: if it shows a defect, or is shattered, or failing [half-ruined], it must either be repaired or pulled down: if collapsed or utterly destroyed, it must be restored, repaired, and renewed from the start.

39. A spacious dwelling makes for a comfortable habitation: one that is cramped and narrower than is right makes for an uncomfortable one.

<margin>

### CHAPTER 53. Concerning the bath and cleanliness.

578. To wash the face often with clear water is merely a matter of cleanliness: but to paint it with rouge or smear it with red pigment is a sign of filthiness. Away with beauty that is false, feigned, borrowed, and acquired through artificial lures!

598. The father begets: the mother, unless she suffers a **miscarriage** $^f$, gives birth, and brings forth **sons** and **daughters**; sometimes she bears **twins** in the same birth (but a **miscarried child** $^f$ does not survive to live):

599. Both of them raise, cherish, and kiss the children, and nurture them in their laps and bosoms.

600. A **stepfather** and **stepmother** do not love their **stepchildren** in the same way as biological parents; because neither is the true parent.

## CHAPTER 58. Of the City.

613. <margin>a Ramparts</margin> Walls, ramparts ^a, entrenchments, and the stakes and bulwarks of the fortification protect the city.
614. The space between <gloss>the interval</gloss> has a ditch; the city boundary <note>original: *pomoerium* — the sacred open space left clear on either side of the walls for religious and military purposes</note> is within, where access to the walls is open to the citizens and townsfolk.

Hidden galleries <gloss>vaults</gloss> are underground rooms.
617. Narrow alleys are for the most part impassable.
618. The town is enlarged by suburbs and decorated with towers, especially if they are walled and gabled.
619. <margin>b They enjoy equal privileges.</margin> Not all the inhabitants of the municipality are privileged ^b; but only the natives, and the fellow-citizens, or those gifted with citizenship.
620. Some of these, being exempt from the census, taxes, and public burdens, live for themselves in private.
621. <margin>c Registered residents.</margin> Foreigners, outsiders, strangers, and tenants ^c are subject to taxes.

626. A basilica is a majestic temple or house.
627. <margin>* From where one can keep watch, or from where a signal is given by lighting a fire of the enemy's arrival.</margin> Lighthouses and watchtowers * should be in a higher place; and let the watchmen keep their watch <gloss>keep guard</gloss>.

### CHAPTER 61. Concerning the Superstition of the Jews and Heathens.

### CHAPTER 62. Concerning the Town Hall.

<margin>519.</margin> In the town hall <note>original: *curia*—the administrative center of a city</note>, on an assembly day <gloss>a legal or business day</gloss>, the Senate hold their meetings and handle the affairs of the state.

<margin>520.</margin> There the register of citizens <gloss>the official list or roll</gloss> and the public records are kept.

<margin>521.</margin> The Consul <note>The chief magistrate or mayor</note> proposes matters for deliberation, the Senators voice their opinions, and he brings the matter to a conclusion.

<margin>522.</margin> The Notary, enclosed within a partitioned desk <note>original: *cancellis septus*—behind a railing or screen, from which the word "chancellor" is derived</note>, records the proceedings; and thus each person performs his duty.

<margin>523.</margin> Their attendants are the Apparitors <note>official servants of the court or council</note>, namely: bailiffs <gloss>messengers</gloss>, ushers, clerks <gloss>record-keepers</gloss>, and heralds <gloss>public criers</gloss>.

<margin>524. † The poorest citizens <note>original: *proletarii* and *capite censi*—literally those "counted by their heads" rather than property</note> are below the standard rank; they are not considered of the first class, nor are they counted among them.</margin> The common people, divided into tribes <gloss>classes</gloss>, have their own leaders <note>original: *tribunos*—tribunes</note>, through whom people's decrees <note>original: *plebiscita*</note> are brought to the senate for confirmation <note>original: *ratihabitionem*</note> as a formal decree of the senate <note>original: *senatus consulto*</note> †.

<margin>525.</margin> The craftsmen also have their own halls or guilds <note>original: *collegia*</note> for the sake of order (so that a newcomer <note>an apprentice or novice</note> who begins to earn a living may present a masterpiece <note>original: *specimen*</note> of his skill to the Wardens <note>original: *Curionibus*—the heads of the guild</note>) as well as their own secret meetings, which are sometimes shameful.

### CHAPTER 63. Concerning Lawsuits and Judgments.

<margin>526.</margin> When two people argue over any dispute, a third party must intervene to settle the lawsuit <note>original: *litem*</note> or decide the matter they are quarreling about; otherwise, the strife and contention would go on forever.

<margin>527.</margin> Either they must settle the matter themselves <gloss>reach a compromise</gloss>, or choose for themselves a respected arbiter <gloss>a mediator</gloss> to whose decision they bind themselves to agree; or they must go to the court <note>original: *forum*</note> and try their case according to the law.

<margin>528. ᵃ He initiates an action against him. * By a citation, which our local lawyers call a "writ."</margin> He who calls an adversary to court and brings a charge <gloss>writes a writ</gloss> against him, arrests and summons * him and sets a day for the trial; he brings him before the Judge <note>original: *Prætorem*—the official who handled legal matters</note> (except on a non-business day <note>original: *nefasto die*—a day when legal proceedings were forbidden</note>), and there alleges his offense and accuses him of harm.

<margin>529. † Unless he pleads illness <gloss>makes an excuse</gloss>. ᵇ A defense. * Sometimes there is also a reply, a rejoinder, and a surrejoinder.</margin> At the request of the plaintiff, the defendant <note>original: *reus*</note> is summoned †: the plaintiff's ᵇ accusation and the defendant's ᶜ defense * are heard by the judges <note>original: *cognitoribus*—those who take formal notice of a case</note> whose duty it is to examine the case; if the defendant does not confess but denies the charge, witnesses are admitted.

## CHAPTER 66. Concerning the Kingdom and the Region.

**685.** A Kingdom is where people of free status are bound together by the bond of statutes <note>laws and regulations</note>.

No one but asks for a law: once asked for, the orders of the kingdom pass it (unless the Prince vetoes it): once passed, it is fixed and recorded [inserted] among the public archives, nor is it unfastened or abolished except by the same lawmakers.

**687.** In his own territory, any magistrate can decree what he wishes: but he ought not to wish for anything except what is publicly advantageous.

### CHAPTER 67. On Peace and War.

**690.** A peaceful state is most desirable: but sometimes, it cannot be maintained except by the force of arms.

<margin>Fellow countrymen and compatriots.</margin>
**691.** Since troublemakers spread secret factions and conspiracies among their own fellow countrymen and fellow citizens; and when they have conspired, they stir up riots and seditions: which, unless they are calmed, the state splits into parties, and internal and deadly [internecine] wars are waged.

**692.** An external enemy breaks in from the outside, against whom a defensive war is necessary.

<margin>After a formal declaration of war <note>original: *clarigatione factâ*</note>.</margin>
**693.** This is announced by a herald <note>original: *fecialem*—a priest-official in ancient Rome who dealt with treaties and declarations of war</note>, or peace is sought through a messenger carrying a staff of truce <note>original: *caduceatorem*</note>, if anyone considers himself unprepared or unequal to the enemy's power.

**694.** One who is un-warlike will presume to wage war [to carry on war] in vain.

**695.** For the preparation for war requires many things: a soldier (who must be conscripted, bound by enlistment pay, armed, and inspected <margin>To be reviewed in a purification of arms <note>original: *armilustrio*</note>.</margin>), provisions, the help of allies, and lavish expenses.

<margin>Food supplies.</margin>
**696.** Therefore, money <note>original: *stips*—a small coin or contribution</note> must be collected in good time, as well as food supplies <margin>provisions</margin>, and those who pay it out must be provided, lest the mutinous stir up trouble.

**697.** Then the army must be gathered and organized into legions, cohorts, detachments, and troops: and over these must be set Decurions <note>leaders of ten</note>, Centurions <note>leaders of a hundred</note>, Rear-guards [adjutants or *optiones*], Masters of the Horse, Tribunes [colonels or *chiliarchs*—leaders of a thousand], and finally over all a Commander-in-Chief, to whom they swear an oath of allegiance <note>original: *sacramentum*</note>.

**698.** Recruits are mixed with veterans; volunteers and dual-armed soldiers <note>those trained to fight on foot or horse</note> join themselves to the infantry or cavalry: camp followers <margin>Menial servants, who on a ship are deckhands.</margin>, soldiers' servants, and grooms are brought in for service.

**699.** There will be enough armor if you are covered by a corselet, a helmet or headpiece, a breastplate, and a shield [an oval shield, a round shield, a light crescent shield, or a buckler]: and truly equipped with those things with which you fight. The arms of the armored cavalry <note>original: *cataphractorum*—heavily armored horsemen</note> are <margin>Impenetrable.</margin> immune to wounds.

**700.** If a naval fleet is equipped [established], it will also require grappling hooks [harpoons] and hooks; so that in a sea battle <note>original: *naumachia*</note> the marines [naval soldiers] may more easily leap into the ship, which they may then pillage and strip bare [plunder].

### CHAPTER 68. On Schools and Education.

**724.** Since it is found that the educated are fit for all things, while the uneducated, on the contrary, contribute little to human society, there is a need for schools (where the unrefined are taught manners and humanity and the liberal arts are learned).

<margin>
a Blockheads <note>original: *fungi*; literally "mushrooms," used to describe dull-witted people</note>.
† Which is a rotten and cold [weak] slander.
</margin>

**726.** For if the former [the student] learns of his own accord, asks questions [seeks] eagerly, and listens attentively; and if the latter [the teacher] teaches willingly, instructs with foresight, and impresses the lessons continually; both will find great delight.

* School fees: tuition.
</margin>

b Creep in.

**729.** He who cares nothing for a warning and does not heed advice should be whipped.

<margin>
c A semi-circle.
</margin>

* An ABC-book, or one with words joined together.
† In a notebook.

**733.** Whatever you wish to commit to memory, reread frequently—not hurriedly, in passing, too hastily, or superficially, but with your mind focused on the subject: it will stick.

**734.** Repeat the lesson in a low voice [silently]; recite and repeat it back...

### CHAPTER 69. Concerning the Study.

738. A suitable place for the Muses is a solitary retreat; into which the student, if he would meditate on anything, may withdraw far from the crowd; where he shall have a library, a desk, and an inkstand (with a brush, a pen-case, and a pen-knife).
739. Let him not stain or defile his little books, but handle them cleanly: he shall not have very many, but select ones; and he shall arrange them throughout <term>shelves</term><note>original: "forulos"</note> <margin>a Compartments</margin> and pigeon-holes.
740. (For to what purpose are numerous volumes divided into so many tomes, whose very indexes or catalog the owner can scarcely, or not even scarcely, read through?)
741. Let him not defile them with blots: no one forbids him to aid his memory by marking <term>asterisks</term> in the margin: indeed, it is well-advised.
742. If anything comes to mind, you will not allow it to vanish; but, lest it escape you, you will note it down immediately, not on scrap paper, but in a <term>parchment notebook</term><note>original: "palimpsestum," here referring to a reusable notebook</note>, and from there into a diary or a commonplace book, which you should keep by you or ready at hand.
743. For one working late by the lamp, a wax candle is more conducive than a tallow candle: to light it, let a tinderbox be present with touchwood and matches; to put it out, an extinguisher.

## CHAPTER 70. On Grammar.

<margin>a He inflects.</margin>
747. The Grammarian writes letters with correct spelling <note>original: "orthographice"</note> (using capital letters only for the beginnings of sentences and for emphasis): he combines two vowels into one diphthong, joins syllables, declines and conjugates words [vocabulary], constructs phrases according to the rules of syntax, not inconsistently; he pronounces speech correctly <margin>a providing the proper account of accent, tone, and meaning.</margin>, speaks purely and in good Latin, and shrinks from un-Latin usage, grammatical errors <note>original: "soloecismo"</note>, and scribbling.

748. The Scribes and the Printer are servants to him: the Printer, taking the type from the compartments, joins them together, places them under the press, prints the books, and delivers them to the Bookbinder [the joiner] to be bound; these the Bookseller sews into volumes fitted with ornamental bosses <note>original: "umbilicis," referring to the decorative ends of scrolls or book-fittings</note> and offers them for sale [puts them out for sale, as vendibles].

## CHAPTER 71. On Dialectic <note>Logic</note>.

<margin>a Of an axiom or proposition.</margin>
749. The Dialectician [Logician], in his reasoning, investigates what can be said about what, and why; he distinguishes ambiguities clearly, declares obscure things plain, compares likes with unlikes, and examines the certainty of any statement <note>original: "effati"</note>.

750. He discusses thorny problems or any theme whatsoever, and is never not arguing subtly; he disputes for and against doubtful questions; he weaves arguments together shrewdly into syllogisms <note>logical formulas where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note>; and he arranges all things in an appropriate method.

### CHAPTER 72. Concerning Rhetoric & Poetry.

<margin>† But not like those who are merely clever with words, who foolishly and affectedly hunt for any sort of decorated trifles of flowery speech. <note>original: "logidædalos... phalæratas flosculorum ineptias"</note></margin>
1. The Rhetorician seeks out formulas of speaking † for the sake of eloquence; he exercises his style, colors his words with tropes (by transferring them from their native meaning to another sense), colors his sentences with figures <gloss>schemes</gloss> (by doubling words and artificially rearranging them for a pleasing sound <term>euphony: the quality of being pleasing to the ear</term>), and finally colors his delivery with gestures.

2. The eloquent Orator, when about to deliver a speech from the platform <note>original: "pro rostris," referring to the speaker's platform in the Roman Forum</note>, introduces himself by sending forth an introduction (though sometimes he begins abruptly, with no previous preface); afterwards he sets forth the case clearly and articulately, then confirms it with valid reasons, and illustrates it with appropriate and copious examples (although he does not dilate or amplify more at length than is proper, nor does he digress from the matter); he intersperses pithy sayings <note>original: "apophthegmata"</note> (but rarely, not crowded together); he refutes and disproves objections exactly, or hurls them back at those contradicting him; he concludes with a closing statement <note>original: "epilogo"</note> as accurate and highly polished as possible, and performs all these things partly by premeditation and partly offhand.

3. Proverbs and adages, as well as comparisons, splendidly adorn a speech: which, if it expresses the matter concisely, is said to be "sinewy" <note>meaning vigorous and direct</note>.

<margin>* Complete, undiminished, and not corrupted.</margin>
4. But the skillful Poet, making bound speech out of <gloss>unbound</gloss> prose, composes * legitimate verses, elegantly arranges rhythms, measures out the meter of songs, and fashions fables <note>original: "apologos"</note>, wedding songs, anagrams, acrostics, epigrams, and satires <gloss>satires</gloss>, and from time to time places a refrain beneath the other verses.

## CHAPTER 74. Concerning Geometry.

757. **T**he Geometrician, as if at play, contemplates figures and measures distances, whether something be near or far off.

<margin>* The diameter, which pierces through the swelling of a sphere, is called the axis.</margin>
758. With a ruler he draws lines (namely straight ones * and those drawn out at length, or slanting ones; not curved [distorted], spiral, or irregular ones); with a square <note>norma: a tool for measuring right angles</note> he draws angles; and with a compass he draws a circle (the middle of which is called the center, and the circuit [enclosure] is called the circumference).

<margin>† A pyramid is equally sharpened from a straight-lined base. A rhombus is equal-sided but oblique-angled. a A roller [cylinder].</margin>
<margin>“ A notch.</margin>
759. A cone is top-shaped and is equally peaked from the underlying periphery; like a cluster of grapes†: a cylinder is smooth and round: the Greek Delta <note>Δ</note> is three-cornered: a cube is squared: a globe is round, convex on the outer surface, and concave on the inner.

760. The circular figure is the most divine and most capable, embracing all things, having nothing offensive, no slit“, no winding, no standing-out ridge, nor any hollowed-out little channel.

761. Every dimension is made by means of the triangle.

### CHAPTER 76. On Optics & Painting.

769. The Optician examines visual rays and visible objects: discerning why some are transparent, others opaque; some clear, others dark: and according to this, he fashions mirrors and eyeglasses.

### CHAPTER 77. On Music.

773. The Musician sings melodies and songs: the lead singer leads the song, through certain measures and intervals [<gloss>musical distances</gloss>], and sometimes <gloss>a</gloss> warbles [<gloss>vibrates</gloss>] the voice: after the preludes, the lute-player, the lyre-player, the flute-players, etc. strike the instruments.
<margin>a Quivers and sounds.</margin>
774. A Symphony is the singing together of many, whose agreement [<gloss>harmony</gloss>] is pleasing, while disagreement <gloss>b</gloss> is harsh [<gloss>out of tune</gloss>]. ## CHAPTER 78. On Astronomy.

778. The **Astronomer** observes the movements of the stars: the **Astrologer** considers their influence and effect <note>In the 17th century, astronomy and astrology were often studied together as related disciplines</note>.

<margin>Those which are movable feasts.</margin>
779. From the calendars [Ephemerides <note>Tables showing the predicted positions of celestial bodies</note>], it is clear that **Easter is separated from Christmas by at least three months; Pentecost is nearly two months from Easter; and from there, Advent is about six months away**.*

<margin>* Carnival is followed by Ash Wednesday, which begins Lent.</margin>
<margin>† With which the Romans began their year.</margin>
780. Those [months] are January, February, March: These are June, July [formerly called Quintilis], August [formerly called Sextilis], September, October, November, and December is the last.

781. Each of these in the Roman Calendar had its own **Calends**, **Nones**, and **Ides** <note>Specific marker days in the Roman month system</note>.

<margin>* There is also the five-year period.</margin>
<margin>** Which, while it inserts February 29th (to make the civil year equal to the sun's periodic motion and to absorb the 5 hours and several minutes remaining beyond the 365 days), makes the year longer than it should be. The Gregorian calculation in the New Style is 10 days ahead of our reckoning.</margin>
782. Within a three-year period, there was the addition of an **intercalary month** [an embolism], that is, a thirteenth lunar cycle: A **Lustrum** [a four-year period] brings back the **leap year**.*

## CHAPTER 79. On Geography.

<margin>† For the torrid and frigid zones are habitable, just like the temperate ones.</margin>
783. The **Geographer** describes the location of regions on a geographical map (even those he has not traveled through himself): which are on the mainland, in islands, or peninsulas (which are attached to the mainland by only a narrow neck): which are coastal, which are in the interior, and in what direction; under which **zone** †, climate, or parallel; toward which they incline, how far they extend in **longitude**, and how far they spread in **latitude**: what neighbors these or those people have, and by what boundaries they are divided and separated from them; and their **antipodes** [those who turn their feet opposite to them].

## CHAPTER 80. On History.

784. When actual deeds are narrated, it is **History**: when they are made up, it is a **Fable**.

785. The Historian recounts the former: he should consider it a capital crime to enter the latter into the records of the annals.

786. And so that it may be clear that they are genuine and not forged, he should record the matter with all its circumstances into his commentaries.

### CHAPTER 81. On Medicine.

787. *The best* medicine is diet: because it is the safest, and without violence.
788. Do not drink or eat <note>original: "veledas," likely a typo for "edenda" (things to be eaten) or "veleas" (desire)</note> unless urged by thirst or hunger (which the saliva moved at the sight of food and the tickling of the palate will indicate); then you shall be healthy and vigorous.
789. Therefore, wait for an appetite while fasting.
790. But even ill health, if it comes upon you, is cured by abstinence and rest: which those do not notice, who do not fast unless they are full, and do not rest unless broken by labor.
<margin>a Phlebotomy, the letting of blood.</margin>
<margin>b Soothed, these are anodynes <note>pain-relievers</note>.</margin>
791. Rubbing, warm compresses, a blood-letting, cupping-glasses, and all things applied from the outside (such as wax-salves, poultices, and softening ointments) do not remove the torment, but they mitigate, soften, and soothe b.
<margin>c Suppositories <note>literally "acorns"</note>.</margin>
<margin>d Electuaries <note>medicinal pastes</note>.</margin>
792. Purgative remedies, evacuants (laxatives, clysters <note>enemas</note>, suppositories c), diuretics and sweat-inducers, strengthening and heart-tonics <note>cardiacs</note>, are more effective and heal the sick more powerfully; whether they be potions to be swallowed, or d pastes to be smeared and licked, or pills [capsules] to be devoured. For eye-inflammations <note>Ophthalmix</note>, eye-salves <note>collyria</note> are beneficial †.
<margin>† Nasal powders <note>Errhina</note> drawn into the nostrils cause sneezing, and draw out mucous phlegm. Emetics provoke vomiting.</margin>
<margin>* Or they are drawn out by the juice of fleawort.</margin>
793. Poisons are driven out by antidotes [alexipharmics]; enchantments by amulets, charms, or incantations, or even by the little word, *No offense intended* <note>original: "Præfiscini," a traditional Roman formula to ward off the "evil eye" or bad luck when praising someone</note>.
794. There is a salty <note>witty/biting</note> taunt against Physicians (would that it were not true!) that they alone are permitted, once the fee <note>original: "sostro"</note> is received, to kill with impunity. Which best fits [suits] the Empirics <note>quacks relying on trial and error</note>, perfume-sellers, and wandering braggarts <note>literally "blowers" or "puffs"</note>.
795. They dispute concerning a universal medicine <note>the Panacea</note>, whether it exists or not.
<margin>† They distribute the mixture composed of many simples <note>herbs</note> into doses.</margin>
796. Their associates are Surgeons, Ointment-sellers, Herbalists, and Pharmacists: these, preparing medicines, ointments, syrups [decoctions], powders, and lozenges [troches], do not confuse and mix them into a heap; but keep each one separately in compartments, cases, boxes, and ointment-chests †. Anatomists perform the dissection of a human corpse, and set up a skeleton.

### CHAPTER 82. Concerning Ethics in General.

<margin>a A slip or error.</margin>
797. **V**irtue consists in the middle ground <note>The Aristotelian "Golden Mean."</note>: vice exists both in excess and in deficiency: for to exceed or to fall short is, in either case, to overstep the bounds.

798. If a sinner sins without foresight, out of thoughtlessness, or through carelessness, it is a fault ᵃ: if done voluntarily, it is a misdeed: if by design, it is wickedness: if maliciously, it is a crime: if it is an enormous act, it is an atrocity: if it is done to cause someone distress, it is perversity.

799. And he who commits [designates] such things is a lost soul [deplorably evil].

<margin>b Furthermore / indifferently.</margin>
800. He who considers it a matter of indifference ᵇ [thinks nothing of it] to act wrongly is a good-for-nothing: he who restrains himself from evil is upright: the man who is in every way undefiled detests and shrinks from everything impure; indeed, he curses it.

<margin>c To break a habit.</margin>
801. A vicious habit creeps in gradually, and is resisted too late once it has grown strong: for once it has taken root, it is hardly ever interrupted, and very rarely indeed is it uprooted. We are torn away and weaned ᶜ from our former customs, to which we have become accustomed, only with the greatest difficulty and much effort.

### CHAPTER 83. Concerning Prudence.

802. **T**o value everything according to its worth, neither more nor less than is right, is the essence of prudence: so that things of no value, trifles <note>original: "titivillitii" — a word for a tiny, insignificant scrap or "shred."</note>, and things of no weight are not highly esteemed.

803. Before you begin anything, it is worth the effort to weigh carefully whether it is to your advantage or not, lest you labor in vain [to no purpose].

804. Therefore, look forward to the end, provide the means: and lest anything should hinder you later, pay attention to the opportunity.

805. For it is the mark of the foolish, the dull, and the mindless to be carried away without pause: of the insane, the stupid, and the senseless to desire forbidden things: of the mad and the raging to undertake impossible things which they cannot achieve: and of the unskilled and the inconsiderate to wander in error or neglect an opportunity.

806. Where a choice is given among many things, one must deliberate for a long time and decide but once: but one should refrain from superfluous things.

807. And whatever you undertake, consult exquisitely and expert... <note>The text cuts off mid-word; likely "experire" (try/test).</note>

### CHAPTER 87. On Self-Sufficiency. <note>original Greek: "Autarkeia"</note>

<margin>a Greed.</margin>
846. The miserly and the greedy man seize by hook or by crook <note>original: "per fas aut nefas," meaning by right or wrong</note>, extorting from others and laboring to grow rich; yet it is the blessing from above that truly enriches.

849. If you have wealth in abundance, help the needy in turn: if not, share even from your modest means—if not bountifully, at least generously.
850. It is better to be generous and munificent than to be stingy.
851. The frugal man is indeed neither grasping nor filthy; but he devotes his effort to thrift; and being content with his lot, he does not envy others their happiness, which he does not desire for himself at all.
852. If the extravagant man could see how great a revenue frugality is, he would not squander his inheritance on luxury [*extravagance*].
853. For waste brings poverty, while saving <note>original: "compendium," a shortcut or gain through saving</note> brings wealth.
<margin>f A tally stick.</margin>
854. Therefore, whatever you receive and spend, record it in a ledger of receipts and expenses, or mark it on a f tally stick. Let your expenses be so far from exceeding your annual income that they do not even equal it.

### CHAPTER 92. On Constancy.

### CHAPTER 94. On Sincerity.

918. With whomever you associate and have a close relationship, be open, without fraud or deceit: for what honor is there in betraying, cheating, or deceiving a friend?

919. Take to yourself a faithful companion, and be faithful to him: do not secretly withdraw <margin>take away</margin> <insert>steal</insert> anything from him; undertake nothing to his detriment: for he who acts treacherously plots his own destruction.

920. If something must be criticized or blamed, let it not be done in secret, but openly, to his face, and with plain-speaking <term>parrhesia: the Greek concept of speaking candidly and boldly</term>, just as you feel, provided it is done at the right time.

921. Nothing is more foreign to friendship than flattery.

922. Do you see a fault? Do not conceal it: remind him, rebuke him, scold him; for why should you pretend not to see it?

923. If a neighbor has done wrong, remind him of his error, openly reprove and correct him: to flatter and stroke a wrongdoer is the mark of shifty impostors.

924. If someone speaks useful things and to the point, agree and give your consent: if they speak useless things or things foreign to the matter, do not play the flatterer.

925. Coaxing and services are the tools of the deceitful: charms, fawning gestures, and reverent bows, and such-like flattering trifles, are the marks of sycophants <margin>Courtly ceremonies</margin> <insert>flatterers</insert> and <insert>cajolers</insert> <margin>Those who speak only to please</margin>; you should do all things with candor and sincerity.

926. Do not be ashamed to confess the truth naturally, as you are a witness to it: for why would you wish to be put under oath?

927. Do not show yourself to be intimate with those whose sincerity has not yet been proven to you: otherwise, you will incur contempt from too much familiarity.

928. Do not try to charm those you do not know, lest they think you are trying to seduce them or make yourself a nuisance to them.

# INDEX OF WORDS.
<note>original: "INDEX VOCABULORUM"</note>

The former *Index*, even in the Dutch copy, was very faulty in the figures <note>original: "cyphers," referring to the reference numbers</note>, and defective in many words; which put me to a needless trouble, in striving to insert in the text, such words as I found not in the *Index* (and therefore thought them lacking) which afterward I met with in the book. This *Index* is very exact; and may serve as a Dictionary to the learner, and a ready help to him that would add any supply to the book itself. Simples <note>root words</note> and words out of rule <note>irregular forms</note>, are set down more at large; others more briefly. Participles, if regular, are referred to the same number with the verb. Irregular compounds have their simples added in a parenthesis. Understand by *m. masculine, f. feminine, n. neuter, c.g. common gender, a. adjective, d. deponent, p. participle, c.f. lacks a supine <note>a specific Latin verbal noun form</note>, pr. in the past tense, v. look <note>original: "v. ei-de," likely a contraction for "vide"</note>, (An adverb hath no mark at all set after it) ib. in the same place <note>original: "ibidem"</note>, that is, in the same number with the next afore-going.*

# Section SE

### SED
**Sed** — But, however. <note>A fundamental conjunction used to introduce a contrast.</note>
**Sedat** — He/she settles, calms, or stills. <note>From the verb *sedare*, meaning to appease or quieten.</note>
**Sedes** — A seat, a dwelling place, or a foundation. <margin>Often used in ecclesiastical contexts to refer to a "See" or throne.</margin>
**Sedulus** — Diligent, busy, or industrious. <gloss>One who acts with care and persistence.</gloss>

<column-break/>

### SEM
**Semel** — Once, or a single time.
**Semen** — Seed, grain, or the origin of a thing. <term>Seminary (a place where seeds of knowledge are planted)</term>
**Semis** — A half, or a portion of a whole. <insert>Also used to denote a small copper coin.</insert>
**Semper** — Always, forever, or continually.

### SEP
**Septem** — Seven. <note>The cardinal number.</note>
**Septum** — An enclosure, a fence, or a partition.
**Sepulchrum** — A grave, tomb, or place of burial. <margin>Derived from *sepelire*, to bury.</margin>
**Sequor** — I follow, I pursue, or I come after. <note>original: "Sequor"</note>

->**End of the SE- Entries**<-

## POEMS BY MURETUS. <note>original: "Mureti Versus"; Marc-Antoine Muret (1526–1585) was a famous French humanist and scholar known for his excellent Latin style. His poems were frequently used in schools to teach both language and morality.</note>

### *To a Student of the Muses.* <note>original: "Musarum Alumno"; The Muses were the ancient Greek goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences. A "student of the Muses" is a dedicated scholar.</note>

*How happy is the boy whose virtue* <note>original: "virtus"; in this context, it refers to both moral character and intellectual excellence.</note> *outpaces his years!*
*Everyone competes to honor him with the praise he deserves,*
*And they watch him with admiration, and pray for his every success.*
*But on the other hand, no one deigns to speak with the idle;*
*They are scorned by everyone and become a cautionary tale* <note>original: "vulgi fabula"; literally "the talk of the common crowd."</note> *for the masses,*
*Hardly even does his own father look upon him with a kind eye.*

*O Blessed child, whose talents* <note>original: "parts"; in the 17th century, "parts" referred to a person's abilities or intellectual capacities.</note> *his age out-run,*
*whose virtues name* <note>original: "stile"</note> *him a man before his full height!* <note>original: "stature"</note>
*Each eye beholds him as the rising sun,*
*each heart applauds him, as a pearl in nature:*
*Indeed, even strangers bless his promising upbringing,* <note>original: "hopefull breeding"</note>
*and breathe out prayers for his happy success.*

*But when fresh-springing buds prove eaten by decay,* <note>original: "canker-fretted"; damaged by a cankerworm, a common Renaissance metaphor for youth being corrupted by vice.</note>
*with the stain of vice, or the rust of immature laziness;* <note>original: "sappy sloth"; "sappy" here refers to the immature energy of a young plant that is not yet firm or productive.</note>
*Their nearest friends, that see their hopes defeated,*
*are reluctant to speak to them kindly, or even deign a look:*
*But view such foul* <note>original: "noisome"</note> *weeds with loathing scorn;*
*Indeed, parents wish such failing plants were never born.*

## CHAP. I. *The Entrance.*

<margin>a Good morning. (This serves as a general greeting for a first meeting.)</margin>
1. $^a$**G**od save you, friendly Reader.
2. If you ask what it means to be a good scholar, take this for an answer: it is to know how one thing differs from another, and to be able to identify everything by its own proper name.
3. Is there nothing more to it? Truly <gloss>verily</gloss> nothing at all.
4. <margin>b How to call, or give a right name to things created by nature, or produced by human skill <note>original: "art"; in this context, "art" refers to "artificial" or man-made crafts and technology.</note>.</margin>

5. But that (perhaps) is a hard <gloss>difficult</gloss> matter.
6. It is so, if a person approaches it with an unwilling mind, or scares themselves with a preconceived notion <note>original: "fore-stalled conceit"; a prejudice or fixed idea formed before actually trying the task.</note>.
7. *But in the end, if there happens to be any difficulty, it will only be at the very beginning.*
8. <margin>c Strange or unnatural.</margin>

10. It is exactly the same with everything: it appears toilsome when viewed from the outside <gloss>appearance</gloss>.

### CHAP. 2. *On the world's origin or beginning.*

18. God created all things from nothing.

19. For in the beginning, He spread out that huge, wide *space* or *room* where heaven and earth exist.

20. And He filled it with a kind of dark and misshapen thick fog.

<margin>a Qualities or other circumstances added to a thing, besides its mere existence.</margin>
21. Out of which, as the matter or *stuff*, He shaped bodily creatures, distinguished by their forms and clothed with various accidents$^a$ <note>In historical philosophy, "accidents" are properties of a thing—like color or smell—that are not essential to its basic nature.</note>; according to the pattern or *blueprint* of every thing He had conceived within Himself.

22. And in every thing He planted its own nature—that is, a power to keep to its own measure <gloss>size</gloss>, kind, and the place assigned <gloss>allotted</gloss> to it.

<margin>A blight or plant-sickness.</margin>

### CHAP. 18. *Of creatures living as well on land as water: and of creeping things.*

## CHAP. 22. *Of the inward parts of the Body.*

266. **W**ell said: let us now look into the bowels or entrails.

<margin>
a Incisors <note>original: "Shearers"</note>.
* Of which the 2 or 3 last are called wisdom teeth, as being grown long after, about the age of 28.
b Animal entrails <note>original: "Tripes"</note>.
</margin>
267. Food [*nourishment*] being minced [*shred*] with the incisors <note>original: "fore-teeth"</note>, and chewed with the molars <note>original: "great teeth" or "grinders"</note> (for the puffing of the cheek acts as the mill) it is let down through the gullet or **esophagus** <note>original: "meazon"</note> to the mouth of the stomach. (In four-footed beasts, it goes first to the rumen <note>original: "cud"</note>, then to the reticulum <note>original: "souse"</note>, next to the omasum <note>original: "panch"</note>, and at length to the true stomach <note>original: "right maw"</note>, called the abomasum <note>original: "Manifold"</note>.) The food is girt in [*crowded, thronged, and pent up*] very close together above and below (the lower mouth of the stomach being closed straight up); where (all being broken small, and passing well mingled and blended) it is mashed or boiled soft by the **first concoction** <note>The historical term for the first stage of digestion in the stomach</note>, and wrought into **chyle** <term>chyle: a milky fluid of partially digested food</term>, appearing like a white creamy pap.

<margin>
* The duodenum <note>original: "stomack-gut"</note>, the jejunum <note>original: "empty"</note>, and the ileum <note>original: "circled-gut"</note>.
† The cecum <note>original: "blind"</note>, the colon <note>original: "collick"</note>, and the rectum <note>original: "strait-on gut"</note>. All which have one through-passage, but are not all of the same bore or width.
c Bowel movement <note>original: "Sieg, clest, arse"</note> are different words for the same act.
</margin>
268. When the chyle is thus prepared, and thrust down into the **small guts** * through the lower mouth of the stomach (which now is untied and opened wider); the **mesenteric veins** <note>original: "mesaraik veins"</note> suck and draw it out. Having severed it from the grosser offals or *refuse* (which being voided out at the **large guts** † and the anus <note>original: "fundament"</note> ^c, turn into dung and stinking waste), they carry it along to the liver (and at the same time ^d carry back blood to the guts); where again there is a division made.

<margin>
d Done simultaneously <note>original: "With one and the same labour"</note>.
e Ureters <note>original: "Pissing-pipes"</note>.
f Urine <note>original: "Lant, stale"</note>.
</margin>
269. The watery part passes to the kidneys or reins (through which it is strained as if through a sieve) and from there through the **ureters** ^e it is dropped into the bladder, and turns to urine or *piss* ^f, which is let out by urinating or *making water*.

270. The fatter part takes a red color from the liver, and becomes a **humor** <note>The four "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were believed to control health and temperament</note> and blood; which is dealt out separately through the veins, and like a jellied dew is glued and cleaves to every part, until it becomes one with that part and passes into the very substance of it.

271. In the meantime, the **milt** or spleen draws **black bile** <note>original: "melancholy"</note> to it, and casts it out again; the gall bladder draws **yellow bile** <note>original: "yellow kholler"</note>.

272. **Phlegm** <note>original: "Fleam"</note> runs about over all parts. **Glands** <note>original: "Kernels"</note> are drainers, through which the overplus of moisture breathes out insensibly.

## CHAPTER 28. Of the Mind.

53. In its search for knowledge, the Mind consults <gloss>seeks counsel from</gloss> Reason, for its goal is to reach a true understanding of the matter.

<margin>" Soon.</margin>
<margin>* Because of the dullness of their apprehension.</margin>
54. Someone with an exceptionally sharp wit <margin>"</margin> quickly perceives <gloss>detects</gloss> a thing; however, dullards <margin>*</margin> <gloss>those of slow wit</gloss> are somewhat slow.

55. He who searches into many things is diligent <note>The original uses "painfull" in the older sense of being painstaking or hardworking.</note>; he who knows them is skillful; he who devises <gloss>finds them out</gloss> them is clever <gloss>cunning</gloss>. He who has confirmed his knowledge through practice and experience is an expert <gloss>highly insightful</gloss>; he who knows how to use his skill as the situation requires is prudent <gloss>wise and discreet</gloss>; he who actually puts it into practice is truly wise; but he who misuses <gloss>misapplies</gloss> it is crafty and deceitful.

56. On the contrary, he who pays attention to nothing is sluggish; he who perceives nothing is a blockhead <margin>† He that merely guesses, surmises, or wavers back and forth is unsettled and unresolved—one who says they "will consider it."</margin>.

57. The understanding of a thing, if it is true, is knowledge; if false, it is an error <gloss>an oversight</gloss>; if weak, it is merely an opinion <gloss>a private fancy or notion</gloss>; if it comes from guessing, it is suspicion <gloss>a surmise</gloss>; if it wavers, it is doubt; if it is obstructed, it is a mistake; if there is no understanding at all, it is ignorance.

<margin>a Are over-ruled by.</margin>
<margin>* When we are stuck and withhold our agreement, it is a reluctance to yield.</margin>
58. When we believe what another person says, that is belief <gloss>faith</gloss>; when we <margin>a</margin> yield to likely reasons, it is persuasion; when we yield to a powerful and clear proof, it is assent <margin>*</margin>.

### CHAP. 29. Of the will and affections.

360. It is the nature of the will to love and desire to have good things, and to hate and reject evil.
361. If these *ill* things please anyone, or those good things displease <gloss>cause discontent</gloss>, it happens by accident <gloss>incidentally</gloss>; for then the appearance <gloss>outward semblance</gloss> deceives the will, so that it chooses the worse or scorns things of which it is ignorant.
362. But look how subject the will is to the emotions <note>The original uses "affections" to mean the passions or emotional states of the mind.</note>! How often it is disordered <gloss>put out of frame</gloss> by them!

<margin>
* This longing fades if there is no desire for them.
a Expecting good fortune.
b A bold or eager intensity.
</margin>
363. When good things are absent, the will misses and desires them; it wishes for *them*, longes after* them, a hopes for the best, exerts itself, endeavors, and busies itself <gloss>stirs itself up</gloss> with all its might; yet for all that, it fears being disappointed.
364. From this arise longings, vows, hope, earnest desires b, attempts <gloss>active effort toward a goal</gloss>, endeavor, and the taking of thought or care.
365. Before it obtains what it wants, it is very impatient to be put off <gloss>delayed</gloss> even for a short time.

<margin>bb Happy or well-pleased.</margin>
366. When good things are present, the will is joyful <gloss>frolicsome</gloss> with earnest longing; it rejoices, it is glad bb, it leaps <gloss>bounds</gloss> for joy, and delights in enjoying them, though it is afraid to lose *them*. From this come mirth, gladness, and pleasure, yet joined with fear.

<margin>c Wishing a thing had never happened.</margin>
367. If they are taken away, the will is sad, it grieves, and complains; hence come sorrow, regret c <note>The original uses "fore-thinking," an archaic term for regret or wishing a past action undone.</note>, complaint, and heart's grief.
368. But evil things cause even more disquiet and distraction to the will.

<margin>d To have a distaste for; wanting nothing to do with it.</margin>
369. For it abhors, dislikes d, and shuns future evils; and yet it fears them, shakes, and is perplexed. From this comes loathing <gloss>regret or aversion</gloss>, fear and dread, trembling, and pensiveness <note>In this context, "pensiveness" refers to a state of anxious or sorrowful reflection.</note>.

<margin>e Shuddering or a ghostly terror.</margin>
370. As evils approach, it fears, quakes, quivers, and trembles <gloss>is startled</gloss> by them, or is astonished and dismayed. From this comes fear, quaking e, and starting <gloss>shivering</gloss>.

## CHAP. 33. Of grinding.

<margin>That is, crushed and husked.</margin>
401. **In** ancient times, people only crushed and pounded grain with pestles in a mortar; because of this, barley-water made of husked and beaten barley was called <term>ptisan<note>A medicinal drink or porridge made from pearl barley; the ancestor of the modern "tisane" or herbal tea.</note></term>.

<margin>A stamping mill or grinding house.</margin>
402. In later times, they crushed the grain with a heavy rammer in a milling house; this was how gruel and <term>frumenty<note>A popular medieval dish made of cracked wheat boiled in milk and seasoned with cinnamon and sugar.</note></term> were made.

<margin>The most recent invention.</margin>
403. Mills were invented last of all; first came hand-mills [**querns**], followed by horse-mills, then water-mills, and finally wind-mills.

<margin>Flour or meal.</margin>
<margin>A hair-cloth sieve.</margin>
404. In these mills, the <term>flower<note>An archaic spelling of "flour," referring to the "flower" or best part of the grain.</note></term> is ground small between the millstones (the upper and the lower stone). It is then sifted and strained through a hair-cloth <term>boulter<note>A device or cloth used for sifting flour; also called a "serce."</note></term>, while the coarse bran is cast out.

405. But the miller who does the grinding is always looking for his <term>toll<note>The portion of grain or flour kept by the miller as payment for his services.</note></term>.

---

## CHAP. 34. Of making Bread.

<margin>A storage bin.</margin>
<margin>A batch of dough.</margin>
406. **The** Baker works in a kneading trough. Using a <term>treen slice<note>A wooden spatula or stirring tool; "treen" simply means "made of a tree."</note></term>, he kneads the lump of dough or paste. When it has been shaped into loaves, he uses a <term>peel<note>A long, shovel-like tool used by bakers to slide loaves into a deep oven.</note></term> to place them into the oven or baking pan.

<margin>Whole grain, just as it comes from the mill.</margin>
407. Leavened bread (made with yeast) has a double crust and a light, puffed-up [**hoaved**] crumb inside. Unleavened bread is dense and solid. <term>Manchet<note>The finest quality of white bread, reserved for the wealthy.</note></term> is made without any bran at all; household bread is made of whole wheat; and <term>bisket<note>A "twice-baked" bread (biscuit) designed to stay edible for long periods, especially for sailors or travelers.</note></term> is made for lasting a long time.

<margin>Fine flour dust.</margin>
<margin>Dumplings or Lenten loaves.</margin>
408. The confectioner [**Sugar-baker**] prepares sweets and delicacies from the finest flour. The various kinds of cakes include <term>simnels<note>A rich, spiced cake, often associated with Mothering Sunday or Easter.</note></term>, rolls, wafers, fritters, pancakes, spice-cakes, buns [**cracknels**], tarts, and dumplings; he also makes meat pasties, apple pies, custards, cheesecakes, and the like.

### CHAP. 39. Of Fowling [birding].

**38.** **T**he Fowler, having set his bird-catching tools, either traps small birds with a net—after they are enticed and lured by bird-calls ^a—or entangles [*hampers*] them with <term>lime-twigs</term> <note>Twigs coated in a sticky substance called birdlime, designed to trap birds when they land.</note>, which he places on a pole or a perch. He may also trap them in the loops [*meshes*] of a ^b <term>springe</term> <note>A snare or trap that snaps shut.</note>, a pitfall, or other mechanical snares [*gins*].

**39.** Those birds he allows to live, he shuts in a cage, either keeping them all together or separately [*each by itself*].

<margin>c Wriggles her foot free.</margin>
**40.** If a bird caught by the leg manages to free herself ^c, she flies away, unless she happens to get caught in the snares once more.

### CHAP. 40. Of Cookery.

**41.** **T**he <term>Caterer</term> <note>The person responsible for purchasing provisions.</note> [*purveyor* ^a] buys the supplies ^b; the <term>clerk of the larder</term> <note>A "yeoman of the larder" was an official in a large household responsible for the meat and pantry stores.</note> ^c brings them out of the store-house. The cook, working at the hearth, boils the meat in cauldrons, pans, brass pots, and kettles [*skillets*] †. He roasts it on <term>spits</term> <note>Long, thin metal rods for rotating meat over a fire.</note> [*broches*] \*, or broils it on a gridiron, toasts it on a roasting-iron, or fries it in a pan.

<margin>“ A pot-spoon.</margin>
**42.** If the pot boils too fiercely, he stirs and cools it down with a ladle “ until the heat subsides [*cools again*]; if a scum forms on the surface, he skims it off with a skimmer.

<margin>d A wicker basket or strainer.</margin>

### CHAP. 41. Concerning the Preparation of Drinks.

<margin>Bends or trains.</margin>
439. **T**HE vine-dresser plants young vines and trains the leading branches from bough to bough; he digs the vineyard with a two-pronged fork, and supports the <gloss>shoots</gloss> with <gloss>props</gloss> or supporters; a little while later he prunes them, and then he gathers the harvest. When the grape-gathering is finished, he leaves the gleanings on the branches for the poor.

440. The <term>vat</term> <note>original: "fat"; a large tub used in brewing or winemaking.</note> presses grapes full of seeds; from which, when pressed, a sweet juice is forced out. This juice is transferred from the <term>cooling-vat</term> <note>original: "keel-fat".</note> into the <term>hogshead</term> <note>A large wooden cask.</note> <insert>which is bound around with hoops to prevent it from leaking</insert>. This liquid is called <term>Must</term> <note>New wine that has not yet fermented; original: "woort".</note>, and after it has <gloss>settled and cleared of sediment</gloss>, it is called wine; a drink well-suited to cheer the heavy-hearted, especially if it is heated with spices.

<margin>Authentic or genuine.</margin>
441. When it is a full year old, it is at its best; if it is from the current year, it is somewhat cloudy. <gloss>Excellent</gloss> wine, though it be old, will remain good for a long time; however, wine mixed with water will soon <gloss>become sour</gloss> and spoil.

<margin>Artificial or imitation.</margin>
442. <gloss>Artificial</gloss> wines include wormwood-wine, elecampane-wine <note>A medicinal wine made from the root of the elecampane plant.</note>, cider, perry <note>A fermented drink made from pears.</note>, and similar drinks.

443. Wine boiled down to a third of its volume is called <term>defrutum</term> <note>original: "defrutum"; a thick grape syrup used as a sweetener or preservative.</note>; when it grows <gloss>sour and past its best</gloss>, it is considered "dead" and has lost its strength.

<margin>Made of water and honey, like metheglin, but stronger.</margin>
<margin>Intoxicating; likely to cause drunkenness.</margin>
444. In places where they do not have a supply of wine, <gloss>Mead</gloss> is brewed; also beer (both weak and <gloss>strong</gloss>), which beer-brewers make from malt and hops, brewing it in a copper cauldron.

<margin>A plug.</margin>
445. It is stored away in cool cellars and sealed with a <gloss>bung</gloss>. Sometimes it is poured from one vessel into another; when it is ready to be served, it is drawn out through a <term>tap</term> <note>The original text distinguishes between the "siphon" (the pipe or faucet that remains fixed) and the "epistiomium" (the cock or spigot that stops the flow).</note> into jugs, just as wine is poured into bottles.

### CHAPTER 44. Concerning Journeys.

<margin>A wayfaring man or traveler.</margin>
<margin>The shortest route.</margin>
<margin>Take no turnings.</margin>
475. Let a traveler go straight on, taking the nearest way to the place he is going, without taking a long detour; let him not turn aside into side-paths.

<margin>A thoroughfare.</margin>
<margin>A guide to lead the way.</margin>
476. Let him not leave the highway (the main road) for an unfamiliar footpath, unless it is a well-beaten track and he has a guide or companions who know the way well.

<margin>Pathless.</margin>
477. He who is afraid of pathless areas and rough, uneven places should not wander away from his path.

<margin>Take the right-hand turn.</margin>
478. A way that has two turns is deceptive; therefore, for fear you might go astray (choosing the wrong way), just at the fork and turning, ask those you meet which way you must go: this way or that way; whether you must turn to the right hand or the left.

<margin>Winding or zigzagging.</margin>
<margin>Crossroads that intersect one another.</margin>
479. Winding ways that go in and out, and cross-roads, do not usually mislead a person as much.

480. So that you may be able to travel without an <term>interpreter</term> <note>Original: "trunchman"</note>, learn exactly the language (the proper speech) of each country.

<margin>A pilgrim or traveler.</margin>
<margin>And wooden clogs or overshoes.</margin>
<margin>A horseman’s coat.</margin>
<margin>A support.</margin>
481. Boots are necessary for one who is to travel abroad; or high-topped shoes for the mud, and a broad-brimmed hat for protection from the sun; a riding coat of leather or of <term>felted wool</term> for the rain; and a walking staff or stick to lean upon, for it provides a support for the hand to rest on.

482. He also needs to have supplies with him for his journey, for expenses, or else <term>letters of exchange</term> <note>Early modern bank drafts or credit notes allowing a traveler to withdraw money in a foreign city without carrying heavy gold</note>.

483. Indeed, he needs patience too; for it happens sometimes that a person must sleep all night in the open air as often as within doors.

484. When you arrive at any city, wherever you are, take good care regarding what company you keep.
<margin>Pickpockets.</margin>
<margin>Vintners and innkeepers [providers of food] make a living off wealthy men, and seek their own profit from other men's losses.</margin>

485. For robbers [*highwaymen*] do indeed steal; <term>pirates</term> <note>Original: "rovers"</note> make prizes of those who go by sea [*robbing them of their goods*]; and even the guest is not safe from his host in his very lodging.

<margin>Small bag or pouch.</margin>
486. Packs [*bundles and parcels*] in which men carry their goods tied up include: a leather pouch, a wallet, a satchel, a cloak-bag, a <term>portmanteau</term> <note>Original: "maile"; a traveling bag designed to be carried on the back of a horse</note>, a pouch, a purse, a pocket, and lastly, a bag and a knapsack.

<margin>Freer from burdens.</margin>
487. So that you may be more agile [*lighter*], do not weigh yourself down [*overload or trouble yourself*] with unnecessary luggage.

<margin>Post-wagons.</margin>
488. If a man is in haste, it is better to use fast horses than <term>post-horses</term> <note>Horses kept at stages along a route for the use of couriers or travelers</note>. Having reached your journey's end, go back [*return*].

<margin>And welcome you home.</margin>
489. When you come back again safe and sound from far away, your friends will welcome you joyfully. There are some who write a journal [*the story of their travel*], recording what happened to them every day.

# CHAPTER 48. Regarding Manual Labor and Trades.

<margin>522.</margin>
<margin>a Green boughs.</margin>
<margin>b Out of all reason.</margin>
In the beginning, dens and caves, huts <gloss>cabins</gloss>, green bowers <gloss>booths covered with leaves <sup>a</sup></gloss>, cottages raised up from green turf <gloss>sods</gloss>, and poor hovels were our dwelling places. <margin>523.</margin>
In some places, these are low; in others, they are lofty, standing two or three stories high or more. These buildings are either the dwellers' own property, or they are hired and rented out <gloss>let to farm</gloss>.

<margin>524.</margin>
Who would live in a narrow, poor cottage by choice?

<margin>525.</margin>
<margin>A wright <note>original: "Faber"</note>: any workman who works with hard materials like iron or wood. A workshop <note>original: "Fabrica"</note> is his forge or shop.</margin>

<margin>526.</margin>
<margin>d Plasters or coats the walls.</margin>
The Mason, using rough stone (made fitting by the stone-cutter) or brick and mortar, builds up the walls using a level and a plumb-line. He fills the gaps between the two sides of the wall with rubble <gloss>filling stones</gloss>. With his trowel, he rough-casts <sup>d</sup> the surface with plaster; specifically using slaked lime <note>Lime treated with water to make it stable for building</note> (not unslaked lime) and with plaster <gloss>parjet</gloss>.

<margin>527.</margin>
<margin>e Chops.</margin>
<margin>e Splinters.</margin>

He cuts the knots <gloss>knurs</gloss> out of the timber; he bores <gloss>thrills</gloss> it, making a hole clean through with his auger <gloss>wimble</gloss> or piercer. He lifts the timber up with pulleys <sup>g</sup>; he builds the partition walls evenly, using laths <gloss>splints <sup>f</sup></gloss> and daubing them with clay-mortar. He makes everything strong <gloss>steadfast and sure</gloss> with driven nails.

<margin>528.</margin>
<margin>h Prevent from being worm-eaten.</margin>

<margin>ⁿ Support or uphold.</margin>
538. Therefore, if a building begins to totter and reel <note>original: "swerve and leane a to side"</note>, it must be ⁿ propped up with a buttress or other supports <note>shores or stays</note>. If it has fallen into decay, shattered, or is ready to collapse, it must be either repaired or pulled down; if it has already fallen or been leveled to the ground, it must be rebuilt entirely from the beginning.

<margin>ᵒ A tenement or rental dwelling.</margin>
<margin>ᵖ Narrower than is appropriate.</margin>
539. A spacious <note>large</note> dwelling-house ᵒ makes for a comfortable home; a narrow <note>overly cramped ᵖ</note> one makes for an inconvenient <note>unpleasant</note> residence.

### CHAPTER 49. *Of a house, and its parts.*

540. When you are ready to enter the front door into a house, to avoid losing your way, stand still in the entrance <note>the porch or portal</note> and look at the front of the building; then knock at the iron door-ring <note>original: "ringel"</note>.

541. If anyone looks out through the lattice <term>lattice: a window frame with diagonal strips of wood or metal</term> or the casement <note>a window that opens on hinges</note>, ask for the door to be opened. If they open it, lift your foot so you do not stumble at the threshold; lower your head <note>stoop</note> so you do not hit or strike it against the lintel <note>the horizontal beam across the top of the door frame</note>. The door-posts <note>door-cheeks or jambs</note> will be on either side of you.

542. Once you have passed through the door, shut it, securing it <note>sparring it</note> with the large bar or at least the bolt, to keep others from coming in.

543. So that the hinges do not grind or the door creak, move them only gently.

<margin>ᵃ Entrance-way.</margin>
<margin>* A fixed set of stairs or a movable ladder.</margin>
<margin>† Spiral stairs joined together around a central post or spindle.</margin>
544. From the front courtyard <note>the hall</note>, an ᵃ entrance opens to other inner rooms. By using plain stairs * or winding stairs †, there is a way to go up to the upper floors <note>lofts</note>.

<margin>* The braces secure the main beams to the upright posts and rest on both.</margin>
545. The roof, which is sloped to shed rain, rests on large beams * <note>wall-plates or principal beams</note>. The tiles, gutter-tiles, or slates rest on the rafters <note>transoms</note>, support beams <note>baufries</note>, and spars; the ends of these beams <note>tenons</note> are fitted into slots <note>mortise holes</note>. The thatched roof-peak <note>ridge</note> is made of straw.

546. External structures <note>additions to the main building</note> include lean-tos and penthouses; there are also overhangs and eaves to direct the rainwater <note>eaves-droppings</note> away, as well as galleries, garrets <note>attic rooms</note>, and balconies <note>terraces</note>.

### CHAPTER 53. Regarding Bathing and Cleanliness.

578. To wash the face somewhat often with clear water is simply cleanliness; to color it with false colors, or to smear it with ^a **makeup**, is a disgusting filthiness. Shame on fake, artificial beauty, which is applied and acquired through a shameful kind of grooming.
<margin>^a Cosmetic paint.</margin>

579. In hot baths, joints that are ^cc stiffened are made supple by bathing in hot or lukewarm water. Bathing places and baths wash away squalor and grime; they clean and scrub away all dirt, sweat, and filth.
<margin>^cc Stiff.</margin>

580. Where, however, for the sake of decency <gloss>comeliness</gloss>, breeches and aprons are used.

581. But dirty clothes are washed by the laundress in a ^b washing tub <gloss>a bucking-tub</gloss> and made clean with lye and soap; or they are brushed with a hair-brush; or wiped clean with a sponge. Collars <note>original: "Neck-bands"</note> are stiffened with starch *.
<margin>^b A large tub used for soaking clothes in lye.</margin>
<margin>* Smoothed with a polishing stone.</margin>

582. We ourselves are rubbed with a coarse hair-cloth and a pumice-stone †; small vessels are rubbed clean with a wisp of straw, or with *horsetail* <gloss>also known as shave-grass</gloss>, or with a bristly brush. Sweepings and scraps are swept away with brooms ^b.
<margin>† A porous stone full of tiny holes used for exfoliating the skin.</margin>
<margin>^b Brooms or brushes.</margin>

583. Where there are no wells <gloss>pits</gloss> that always hold water (out of which, being surrounded by a rim, a man may draw water using a lever-well <note>original: "swipe"</note> and a scoop or a bucket), it is necessary that conduits be made through pipes and water-courses, or through channels <gloss>gutters</gloss>.

584. <margin>^cc Tweezers or nippers.</margin>
