952. A stage-player acteth the person of another man, and playeth interludes [*stage-plays*].

953. A Comedy doth livelily set forth an entangled [*troublesome*] state of a business, but with a joyful upshot: a Tragedy hath a sad [*sorrowful*] ending.

<margin>† Who cheer up or encourage some of the actors; and others they hiss off the stage.</margin>
954. The stage is in the open view: the tiring-[*withdrawing*]-room <note>The dressing room where actors "attire" themselves.</note> (out of which they come forth on the stage to act) is veiled [*over-hanged*] with curtains, provided of attire [*furniture*] for the actors, and not to be seen of the lookers on †, unless the hanging be drawn aside.

<margin>q Mummers <note>Performers in folk plays, often masked.</note>.</margin>
955. They keep Bacchus-feast [*shrovetide* <note>original: "Bacchus-feast"; a reference to Carnival or Shrove Tuesday festivities involving drinking and masks.</note>], being masked q, or disguised with vizards <note>Masks.</note> on.

## CHAPTER 97. Of Death and Burial.

956. **A deadly snoring or snorting** <note>This refers to the "death rattle," the labored breathing of a dying person.</note> is an occurrence that properly happens to men who are ready to die. They who lie drawing their last breath are given over for dead <gloss>as past hope of life</gloss>.

<margin>
a Perishing, decaying.
b Where is that man?
</margin>
957. O ye $^a$mortal men! $^b$What one of a thousand among you takes into account that upon this moment here depends everlasting time?

958. For as soon as thou shalt have given up the ghost <note>The spirit or soul.</note>, the soul shall immediately flit <gloss>remove</gloss> to heaven, or to the torments of hell.

959. **A dead corpse** being set forth with funeral rites (that is, embalmed, wrapped up in a winding sheet <note>A shroud for the body.</note>, put in a coffin, clad in mourning, and laid on a bier) is carried out to the burying by the bearers.

960. The funeral is kept, and the train <note>The funeral procession.</note> goes along toward the churchyard <gloss>burying-place</gloss>, with a show <gloss>all solemnities</gloss> befitting a funeral.

961. The dead corpse <gloss>lifeless carcass</gloss> is buried: we inter it <gloss>put it into ground</gloss>: they of old <note>Referring to Roman or Greek antiquity.</note> made a bonfire, and therein burnt it (*from thence it was that graves or burying places were called burning places*) <note>original: "bustum," a Latin term for a funeral pyre or grave site</note>: and the grave-makers buried the ashes of the dead in a pitcher <note>An urn.</note>.

<margin>
d Ditties.
</margin>
962. Gravestones <gloss>tombs</gloss> and hearses <note>In this context, a framework over a coffin or a monument, rather than a vehicle.</note> are reared up, and epitaphs <gloss>inscriptions</gloss> written on them; and mournful $^d$anthems are sung.

<margin>
e The time of heathenish religion.
</margin>
963. In $^e$heathenism <note>Non-Christian antiquity.</note>, mourning women being hired, kept a wailing, and, with blubberings and mourning songs, reckoned up the praises of them that were gone to the other world (as the heathen use to say).

<margin>
f The day one dieth on.
</margin>
964. And lest their ghosts should walk or *wander*, being all in black, they used dirges or sacrifices for the dead, made to the gods below <note>The deities of the underworld, such as Pluto or Hades.</note>, with feasts at the hearse: keeping a $^f$death-day as well as a birthday.

<summary>This chapter describes the transition from the final moments of life to the various customs of burial, contrasting contemporary Christian practices with ancient "heathen" funeral rites like cremation and professional mourning.</summary>

### CHAP. 98. _Of Gods Providence._

965. **T**hus death maketh an end of all things.

<margin>a That last but a time.</margin>
966. For all things <sup>a</sup> temporal <note>original: "temporall"</note> are unsteady, fading and flitting: they spring up, and they die.

<margin>b Continuance of time.</margin>
967. If peradventure some few things seem sure and steadfast, yet in <sup>b</sup> time they cannot choose but be worn and fall away by very age or oldness.

968. All things are subject to sudden turns <insert>changes</insert>.

<margin>c Infallible, unalterable.</margin>
969. For all that, he is an Atheist <insert>a miscreant</insert> <note>In this period, "miscreant" often meant a literal misbeliever or infidel rather than just a villain.</note>, who weeneth <note>thinks or imagines</note> that our affairs are tossed about at random <insert>at a venture</insert>, and hand-over-head (like moats in the Sun running all of a heap, and skipping up and down,) or, All things follow one upon another by an <sup>c</sup> unavoidable necessity.

970. Chance, hap-hazard, and luck are nothing at all.

<margin>" Fore-sight.</margin>
971. There are indeed, I grant, casual and unexpected <insert>unlook'd for</insert> chances, but in regard of us, not of Gods <sup>"</sup> Providence, which ordereth even the smallest things at his beck.

<margin>d Told.</margin>
<margin>e Perish, or be lost.</margin>
972. For our Saviour witnesseth, that even the hairs of our head are <sup>d</sup> numbered; that not so much as one of them can <sup>e</sup> miscarry.

973. For that reason, before unusual changes, there go strange sights and monstrous wonders.

<margin>f Fore-warnings.</margin>
974 Therefore there are in things, foretokens <sup>f</sup> <insert>signs to guess by, that bode good or ill</insert>, by which being fore-warned let us be fore-armed.

<margin>* As sneezing, bleeding at the nose, and the like to these.</margin>
975. But to catch all about, at any thing *, for a sign of good luck or bad <insert>to say, My mind gives me, or mis-gives me</insert>: away with this superstition from Christians. If the LORD shall vouchsafe to reveal or make known any thing to thee, thou shalt not be ignorant of it.

<margin>g Abandon.</margin>
976. Be thou godly <insert>devout</insert> and pray; he will not utterly <sup>g</sup> forsake thee, who hath as well fore-ordained *what shall become of thee to-morrow, what the next day after to-morrow, and so afterwards; as what was done yesterday, what the day before it, what t’other day, and so many years ago.*

### CHAPTER 100. *The Conclusion.*

1. Tell me, I pray thee, what remains behind? for the things thus far delivered (be it spoken without boasting) I have in some reasonable sort attained <gloss>gotten</gloss>.
<margin>God send thee good of it.</margin>
<margin>Wicket <note>A small door or gate, often used metaphorically for the entrance to knowledge.</note>.</margin>
<margin>The writings of Philosophers and Divines.</margin>
<margin>A snatch and away.</margin>
2. Sayest thou so? Bravely done! <insert>Well may it thrive with thee.</insert> Go on cheerfully <gloss>with a courage</gloss> in this thy diligence <gloss>earnestness</gloss>. It now remains, that going in at this <insert>little gate</insert> <gloss>entry-door</gloss> thou hasten lustily, to take a thorough survey of the Palaces both of arts, and of pure Latin speech; and view those things more plentifully in <insert>good authors</insert>, which here thou hast beheld by <insert>snatches</insert>, and in haste.
<margin>And the study of language, and civil learning.</margin>
3. Here hast thou briefly <gloss>shortly</gloss> and closely trussed up a short <gloss>brief</gloss> comprisal, being as it were the first bare grounds as well of Philosophy <insert>as Divinity</insert>. I suppose, that nothing is over-slipped, so far as I know; nor have I willingly balked or waived any thing.
4. Now to cast in this for a vantage, I would wish thee to turn and apply every whit to godliness.
5. For know, that ere long it will come to pass, that we must give up an account of all things; to wit, when he shall come to raise us up and judge us, where things hidden and manifest shall all be laid open.
<margin>Favouring their cause, well-pleased.</margin>
6. O blessed men, which then shall have him <insert>reconciled</insert>! they shall be fed with bread of heaven, and Angels food for evermore.
